candidates.title: Large Language Models in Archaeological Practice: Efficacy, Ethics, Risks, and Governance
candidates.abstract: This narrative review examines large language model (LLM) assistance with archaeological literature, code, metadata, and transcription, together with the ethical, legal, and governance conditions on its use. I propose a Zotero Model Context Protocol (MCP) citation-review sequence that records the publication version, source evidence, provisional assessment, and review status. A small case study tests source reading with sixty constructed claims about ten randomly selected papers cited in this manuscript. Ten model-and-reasoning configurations assessed the claims against my human reference judgments. Exact label agreement ranged from 80.0% to 100.0%, with nine configurations matching at least 58 of sixty labels. One evaluator reported the correct source values but selected the wrong label; a matching label could also accompany an inadequate page locator. The study used a controlled PDF interface, one human reviewer, and one run per configuration, and did not test the full Zotero workflow. I recommend establishing permission to process research materials and checking outputs against inspectable evidence. LLM-supplied citations require human source review; citations selected through the author’s own reading can receive an LLM audit, with human follow-up on disagreements, unresolved support, and proposed changes.

candidates.title: In RAG We Trust? Measuring Robustness of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Under Post-Retrieval Context Tampering
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a language model in retrieved documents, and that grounding is also an attack surface: an adversary who edits retrieved text, without touching the model or the retriever, can feed the model fluent falsehoods. We measure this on a 4-bit Llama 3.1 8B system with a MiniLM retriever over FEVER evidence. This version replaces the measurement rather than reinterpreting it. The earlier sweep contained an off-by-one that made a zero-corruption cell impossible, so the row published as a clean baseline carried one corrupted passage; a seeded re-run of 1,911 generations supplies a real control, logs how many passages each corruption rule actually modified, and adds closed-book and irrelevant-context arms. Three results follow. Scored on corruption actually applied, the fooled rate runs 0.4%, 35.7%, 54.0% and 72.0% for zero through three corrupted passages, the zero cell being an internal control with no adoption at all. The rules do not deliver the corruption they request: asked for three passages, numeric substitution achieves it in 6% of cells, so the three rules were never comparable and we withdraw the ranking we previously published. Controls reframe the rest, since the generator is more accurate with no context (83.7%) than with clean retrieved context (77.6%), and with irrelevant context it abstains on every question rather than using knowledge it demonstrably has.

candidates.title: Permission Withdrawal in Tool-Using Language Model Agents: Runtime Enforcement and Recovery
candidates.abstract: AI agents that operate external tools can continue acting after a user narrows their permissions, creating a security problem that final-state evaluation may fail to detect. Existing agent benchmarks commonly emphasize task completion or resulting state, but those outcomes do not reveal whether an unauthorized operation was proposed, approved, dispatched, or merely prevented by a downstream error. We investigate permission withdrawal as a trajectory-level authorization problem and evaluate whether runtime gates can preserve revised permissions while allowing agents to complete work that remains authorized. Two acting models were tested in a deterministic tool environment under prompt-only execution, a rule-based reference gate, and a model-based gate. A 72-episode diagnostic examined two previously exposed write workflows, followed by a separately frozen 384-episode extension spanning eight new tasks and four authorization mechanisms. In the diagnostic, prompt-only agents executed forbidden same-value writes in two episodes; both runtime gates prevented forbidden execution, although the model gate falsely rejected three authorized calls. In the extension, 346 of 384 episodes completed safely and 383 preserved the required protected state. No forbidden request executed successfully, yet the model gate approved three unauthorized requests that were stopped only because the referenced resources did not exist. The results demonstrate that correct final state and zero forbidden execution can still conceal failures in authorization reasoning. We contribute a replayable evaluation framework that separates proposals, gate decisions, dispatch, state transitions, and useful completion, enabling more precise assessment of security controls for tool-using agents.

candidates.title: Large Language Model Framework for Structured Biomarker Extraction and Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Identification From Pathology Reports: Development and Evaluation Study
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive molecular subtype of breast cancer that needs to be identified accurately from pathology reports to inform decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) have been reported to show great potential in the automatic extraction of important oncology information from unstructured medical text. Objective We aimed to create and test an LLM-based approach for automatic biomarker extraction and TNBC subtype classification based on breast cancer pathology reports using prompt-engineering techniques. Methods In total, 532 breast cancer pathology reports from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) were used. Our approach extracted structured oncology features, such as estrogen receptor status, progesterone receptor status, HER2 status, tumor size, tumor grade, and tumor histology, which were used to identify TNBC. We tested 4 frontier models: GPT-4o mini (released July 18, 2024), GPT-4.1 nano (released April 14, 2025), GPT-5 nano (released August 7, 2025), and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite. Results The designed framework was able to extract relevant biomarkers and clinicopathological attributes from unstructured pathology reports and allowed for the automated identification of patients with TNBC. Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite showed superior performance in the extraction of clinicopathological attributes. For all models investigated, chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting was shown to outperform other strategies, such as zero-shot and few-shot prompting, for both biomarker extraction and TNBC classification. GPT-4o mini using CoT prompts reported the highest performance for TNBC classification. Conclusions Using prompt-engineering techniques based on LLMs proved to be an efficient method of translating unstructured breast cancer pathology reports into structured clinical information. Moreover, it can be used to accurately identify the TNBC subtype.

candidates.title: Assertion without a Speaker: Testimony, Tracking, and Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large language models produce assertion-shaped outputs that often bring their users to true belief. I argue for two conclusions of different strengths: that on the best current evidence, these systems do not transmit testimonial knowledge and that hearers are not now positioned to accord their outputs testimonial uptake, which does not wait on the first. From Burge, Williamson, Goldberg, Faulkner, and Lackey, I derive a Tracking Minimum: a source transmits testimonial knowledge that p only if the truth of p , or the evidential support for p , figures in the explanation of its producing that assertion, and does so in virtue of the source’s own production process rather than of a proxy on which that process depends. It is this endogeneity requirement, not any modal profile, that the five accounts share and current systems fail. The argument engages Burge’s extension of his framework to computational sources, the interpretability literature, and the published case for AI testimony, whose dispute with mine turns on an empirically decidable question, for which an experiment is specified. The positive proposal places LLM outputs within an extended epistemology of instruments, with a result that has gone unremarked: a working barometer satisfies the condition these systems fail.

candidates.title: Two-stage synthetic-to-real transfer learning for automated mammography report generation using vision-language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract We present a two-stage synthetic-to-real training pipeline for automated mammography report generation, together with a controlled, preregistered evaluation of whether its synthetic pretraining stage contributes to final report quality. Automated mammography report generation is constrained by the scarcity of paired mammogram-report data: public collections such as VinDr-Mammo and CBIS-DDSM provide structured annotations but no free-text reports. The pipeline converts BI-RADS annotations into synthetic reports (400 generated, 390 retained) to pretrain MedGemma-4B with multimodal LoRA, then fine-tunes on 407 real DMID reports. On the leak-free DMID test subset ( $$n = 49$$ ) it reaches ROUGE-L 0.656, METEOR 0.666, CIDEr 0.649 and BERTScore 0.917, exceeding every external baseline, including the published state of the art. The evaluation then shows that synthetic pretraining does not produce these numbers: the apparent advantage was measured between models of unequal adapter capacity, and at matched capacity the two schemes are equivalent. Across 60 training runs over three corpus sizes, three capacities and five initialisations, against a margin fixed in advance, no configuration favours two-stage training; capacity alone reproduces the gap. Two findings bear on evaluation. Under an assertion-level criterion no model fabricates findings on normal studies; the failure mode is omission. Textual and clinical quality diverge within one model: where two-stage training gains 0.058 ROUGE-L, BI-RADS agreement and sensitivity both fall. With agreement never exceeding $$\kappa = 0.14$$ , the obstacle to clinically useful reporting is diagnostic accuracy, not fluency.

candidates.title: PIX2DB: Reconstructing Executable Relational Databases from Document Images with a 2B Vision-Language Model
candidates.abstract: Abstract Tables trapped in screenshots, scans, receipts and charts are usually extracted as markup that keeps the layout but not the relational meaning: merged cells stay merged, an invoice header and its line items stay unrelated, and “$1,250.00” stays a string. We study image-to-database reconstruction: given one image, produce a SQLite dump whose schema, column types, keys and rows load and can be queried as they are. Training data with exact gold databases is obtained in two ways: by rendering samples of the Spider databases at six layout levels, and by converting PubTabNet, FinTabNet and CORD annotations under the same normalization rules. A 2B model (Qwen3-VL-2B with LoRA) trained on 36,589 pairs and followed by a deterministic verify-and-repair layer reaches 0.86 table exact match and 0.99 foreign-key recall on rendered tables from unseen databases, against 0.75/0.75 for the 8B model of the same family prompted for SQL and 0.47/0.00 for an 8B HTML-to-SQLite pipeline. On held-out real images it obtains cell F1 0.81 (PubTabNet) and 0.96 (FinTabNet) and recall 0.93 on CORD receipt photos. On TabRecSet, a source not used in training, it is the best system that writes a database directly (0.52) but trails the 8B HTML pipeline (0.58), mostly in reading text from photographs. A variant trained on synthetic data alone matches the synthetic score and fails on real images, which locates the value of the real data. Code, model, data and all evaluation outputs are public.

candidates.title: Taming the 8-Billion Parameter Model on a low-cost GPU card for Retrosynthesis
candidates.abstract: We explored the use of post-training quantization (PTQ) to enhance the efficiency of reasoning language models for chemical retrosynthesis in drug discovery. We specifically evaluated the RetroDFM-R model, demonstrating that reducing numerical precision to 4-bit significantly lowered GPU memory requirements while lowering Top-1 accuracy by only about 2 percentage points (3–4% relative) for NormalFloat-4 (nf4) and double-quantized nf4 (nf4dq). The accuracy for 8-bit quantization (int8_ao) was equivalent to the original model but reduced energy consumption by about 17% when only one prediction was required. By testing various quantization methods across different hardware configurations, the study revealed that these techniques allow complex chemical predictions to run on budget-friendly, consumer-grade GPUs. In the augmented setting the 4-bit models returned more distinct candidates, which raised Top-10 accuracy on the full test set by up to 0.8 percentage points; on reactions for which every model filled ten candidate positions, the original model remained the most accurate. In summary this study presents the first evaluation of PTQ applied to RetroDFM-R, a reasoning language model, for chemical retrosynthesis. Ultimately, the research suggests that quantization is a vital tool for making advanced chemoinformatics tools accessible to academic researchers who can run it on cards with smaller GPU memory and can reduce the energy per molecule by about 17 - 30% in the default setting, although it increases it by 30–35% in the augmented setting.

candidates.title: Readability of National Surgical Consent Forms: Artificial Intelligence Generation Versus Simplification
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Consent forms often exceed the reading ability of populations they serve. Large language models may improve accessibility of patient‐facing information, but existing research has predominantly assessed de novo generation, with limited benefit. AI‐assisted simplification of existing, clinically validated material represents a distinct workflow that remains underexplored. This study compared the readability of all 64 consent forms published by NHS England's Getting it right first time (GIRFT) with matched de novo AI‐generated and AI‐simplified versions across six surgical specialties. Methods For each procedure, two AI counterparts were produced using Claude Opus 4.8 with standardised prompts: a de novo AI‐generated form and an AI‐simplified version derived from the original (192 documents across three paired arms). Readability was assessed using five validated metrics, Flesch reading ease (FRE) and word count. Primary outcomes were average reading age (RA) and grade level (GL). Achievement of the nationally recommended RA (≤ 11 years) was also assessed. Results Original GIRFT forms required a mean RA of 16.39 ± 0.85 years. AI‐generated forms were harder to read (17.65 ± 0.73 years, p < 0.001), whereas AI‐simplified forms were easier (13.27 ± 0.67 years, p < 0.001). No form achieved a RA ≤ 11 years. FRE ≥ 50 was achieved by 100% of AI‐simplified, 45.3% of originals and 15.6% of AI‐generated forms. Conclusions De novo AI‐generation reduced readability relative to nationally standardised consent forms, whereas AI‐simplification improved readability. Neither approach achieved the recommended reading age. AI may therefore have a role in improving the accessibility of existing consent forms, but outputs require objective readability assessment and clinical validation before implementation.

candidates.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Method (PEFT) for Bloom’s Taxonomy based Automatic Question Generation
candidates.abstract: In any personalized learning systems and intelligent tutoring systems automatic assessment is an important aspect. Yet research regarding such systems that are designed specifically to test the cognitive complexity of learners are scarce. This research addresses the gap by experimenting the integration of Bloom’s Taxonomy with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for Large Language Models (LLMs). Four PEFT methods – LoRA, IA3, Prefix tuning and Prompt Tuning were implemented, analyzed and tested against a dataset with generated and reference questions. These questions were categorized across six of the standard Bloom’s taxonomy such as Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate and Create (BT1-BT6). Questions are generated from passages retrieved from lecture notes and evaluated with topic-held-out cross-validation, overlap metrics and a Bloom-level classifier. Fine tuning of the models raised the accuracy from 0.20 to 0.58-0.6. A full fine-tuning, LoRA and IA3 did not differ reliably in Bloom classification Accuracy. Retrieved passages improved text similarity for every method but changed Bloom accuracy differently across methods. The results suggests that IA3 gave comparable Bloom accuracy with 0.45% and 0.045% of the parameters. Prefix tuning produced degenerate outputs and prompt tuning did not converge, so neither was ranked, Understand and Apply levels were the hardest levels. This study highlights the potential of PEFT based models to reduce educators' workload by generating an unlimited number of pedagogically aligned questions from instructional content. It also benefits self-regulated learners seeking extensive practice to achieve skill mastery.

candidates.title: A VERIFICATION-CENTRED FRAMEWORK FOR GENERATIVE AI-ASSISTED CODE GENERATION, TESTING, AND DEVELOPER PRODUCTIVITY
candidates.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is changing software engineering by assisting with code completion, function synthesis, test generation, debugging, documentation, and code transformation. These capabilities can reduce routine effort, but model-produced code may contain functional defects, insecure patterns, outdated API usage, or plausible explanations unsupported by execution evidence. Productivity gains therefore depend on more than generation speed: they must be assessed alongside correctness, test adequacy, maintainability, security, and developer understanding. This paper proposes a verification-centred framework for integrating GenAI into software engineering workflows. The framework combines task and repository context, model-assisted generation, static analysis, automated tests, security checks, human review, and feedback telemetry. It defines evaluation dimensions and a reproducible protocol for comparing conventional and AI-assisted workflows without treating acceptance or subjective confidence as substitutes for correctness. The paper synthesizes established research on code generation, benchmark evaluation, automated program repair, test generation, and developer studies. It also specifies metrics for functional pass rate, test coverage, review effort, change size, defect density, security findings, and task completion time. Since no model API, repository, or experiment log was supplied with the title, this manuscript does not invent measured productivity improvements or claim to have run a comparative LLM experiment. Instead, it provides a publication-oriented conceptual framework, a system architecture, equations, and an experimental design that can be implemented with public benchmarks such as HumanEval or repository-level tasks. The central argument is that GenAI produces dependable engineering value when generation is coupled to executable verification, transparent limitations, and accountable human oversight.

It includes 1,296 real-input tasks from six anonymous pond clusters, frozen prompt-condition outputs, 144,000 saved outputs from the synthetic mechanism evaluation, summary tables, and verification scripts. The real-input reference modes are derived from the registered production-rule version and are not independent agronomic gold labels. The package does not include raw prompts, source-record keys, workbook names, exact dates, field images, partner identities, or a complete environment for rerunning every model inference. The six pond clusters cover two study sites. No production/yield outcomes are included. The archive is a saved-output analysis package and does not include the later independent safety validation, which has not yet been conducted.

candidates.title: AI-Based PDF Chat and Summarization Engine Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Dr. Sushma Zade Prof. Dr. Aniruddha Rumale
candidates.abstract: Portable Document Format (PDF) files are the most common way of storing reports, research papers, manuals, and legal documents, but their layout-oriented structure makes them difficult to search and to query conversationally. Large Language Models (LLMs) can answer questions fluently, but they may hallucinate and cannot process long documents that exceed a fixed context window. This study presents the design, implementation, and preliminary testing of a PDF chat and summarization system based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The system uses a three-stage data pipeline (raw, processed, and RAG-ready) that parses PDFs, removes repeating headers and footers, converts content to Markdown, and applies structure-aware chunking, which attaches section-path metadata to every chunk. Answers are generated by the openai/gpt-oss-120b model (served through the Groq API) using passages retrieved from a local ChromaDB vector store with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings, and are returned with page references. Three chunking strategies (fixed-size, Markdown-aware, and hierarchical) are defined, and an evaluation protocol based on answer accuracy, faithfulness, hit rate at k, unsupported-answer rate, and response time is specified for comparing them. In preliminary testing, the system processed uploaded PDFs and answered natural-language questions with an average response time of approximately 2–5 seconds. A full comparative evaluation is left for future work. The study provides a reproducible, small-scale baseline that student and small-team developers can extend, and it argues that document preprocessing and chunking quality are central to the reliability of PDF question answering

candidates.title: Secure Multi-Agent Collaboration Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: As Large Language Models have emerged and become increasingly significant, the way to develop smart multi-agent systems has been transformed, enabling them to communicate, collaborate and decision more efficiently. These systems rely on agents working independently which need to effectively and safely coordinate their actions, to maintain reliability in messy realworld environments. However, bringing LLMs into the mix introduces new risks like data leaks, trickery from bad actors, and trust issues. This paper breaks down a full plan for keeping multi-agent teamwork secure when using LLMs. We look at everything from how they are built and the rules they use to communicate to the safety tools used to stop attacks. We also talk about where this is being used now, the hurdles we still face, and where the tech is headed for building secure AI ecosystems

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Urdu Islamic Jurisprudence: A Review of Design Choices and a Reference Architecture
candidates.abstract: Questions about Islamic law need exact answers with sources. A wrong citation is a serious failure. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fits this need, but Urdu is a low-resource language and there is little guidance for building such a system. This paper reviews the design choices behind an Urdu Fatawa RAG system and proposes a reference architecture. We compare Urdu-capable language models, embedding models, tokenizer cost, vector databases, primary data stores, and backend frameworks against four requirements: faithfulness to sources, precision on close jurisprudential terms, Urdu fluency, and private self-hosting. We argue for chunk-level storage of question-answer pairs, hybrid dense and sparse retrieval fused by reciprocal rank fusion, a prompt with English instructions and an Urdu output example, and a three-container deployment that separates inference, vector search, and the API. Our choices rest on published benchmarks, not on a controlled comparison on our own corpus, and some remain hypotheses. We state which ones, and we give an evaluation plan.

candidates.title: Large language models for multimodal clinical predictive modeling: a systematic review
candidates.abstract: The electronic health record (EHR) comprises structured and unstructured data, both of which are integral for comprehensively representing patient history. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has enabled the incorporation of unstructured data modalities into machine learning models that leverage EHR data. In this systematic review, we characterize studies that utilize LLM-enabled multimodal predictive modeling with EHR data. Following a screening of 641 studies, 57 met inclusion criteria. We identified three strategies for LLM-based multimodal integration: embedding, extraction, and text fusion. Delineated by the format of the unstructured data at the time of fusion, all strategies yielded performance gains (average 6.4% increase) over single modality models. LLMs facilitated modeling by generating note-embeddings for downstream prediction, extracting clinically informative variables, and summarizing long text documents prior to integration. Building on our review, we identified LLM-enhanced predictive modeling considerations that include sample size, interpretability, and computational costs. This study supports the potential value of LLMs for EHR-based predictive modeling and provides a framework for future multimodal modeling tools.

candidates.title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model
candidates.abstract: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.

candidates.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality
candidates.abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.

candidates.title: Newly Important Is Not Newly Built: What Reasoning Post-Training Adds Inside a Language Model, Why the Evidence Separates Representation From Wiring From Deployment, and the Cross-Model Tests That Would Show an Attention Head Is New
candidates.abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Reasoning models are built by post-training a pretrained model with supervised fine-tuning on teacher traces, with reinforcement learning against a verifier, or with both, and a running dispute asks whether this builds new machinery or redirects machinery the base model already had. A 2025 circuit study gave the first side a concrete form: attention heads that are absent from the base model's reasoning circuit and present after post-training, many of them after distillation and supervised fine-tuning, fewer and less stable after reinforcement learning. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that "new" has at least three separable meanings inside a model - a new representation, new wiring that consumes a representation, and a new policy for when existing behaviour is deployed - and that the measurements now in the record each speak to one of them. A head that enters a thresholded attribution circuit is newly important; whether it is newly built is a further question that the comparison as run cannot answer, because the reference model differs from the distilled model's actual parent, the circuit is defined by contrasting the two models' own response styles, and zero-ablation effects in the same study do not separate emergent heads from base-circuit heads or from heads taken from an unrelated task. The strongest cross-model evidence points to a regime split at the level of deployment: base-model steering vectors directed by the thinking model's own gating recover about 76% of the accuracy gap for reinforcement-learned models and about 11% for distilled ones, and a gap-matched pair computed from that study's table preserves the split. At the level of representation, a direction taken from the base model drives backtracking in a distilled model but not in the base. The paper consolidates these values in two tables and a figure, gives a classification procedure, and names five cross-model tests that would show whether a post-training head is new.

candidates.title: MAPS: Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning for Regulating Search Momentum in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by retrieving external knowledge. Recently, some RAG methods interleave reasoning and retrieval, enabling LLMs to progressively generate sub-queries and retrieve external knowledge. However, these methods may suffer from redundant or ineffective sub-queries and insufficiently diverse query exploration. Moreover, due to the tightly interleaved nature of reasoning and retrieval, it remains unclear how the evolving reasoning process influences query intent. To characterize the evolution of query intent during reasoning, we introduce search momentum, which captures the accumulated retrieval tendency induced by historical changes in generated sub-queries along the reasoning trajectory. Through momentum-based analysis, we find that the query generation process tends to continuously evolve along existing retrieval trajectories. Based on this observation, we propose MAPS, a Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning framework for regulating search momentum and mitigating query-intent drift. MAPS first retains the retrieved knowledge and a refined reasoning state, thereby reducing the influence of historical reasoning trajectories on subsequent sub-query generation. Subsequently, MAPS extends the conventional sequential reasoning process into a parallel reasoning paradigm. At each iteration, MAPS identifies complementary retrieval directions, generates corresponding sub-queries for parallel retrieval, and consolidates the retrieved evidence to update the knowledge and reasoning states. Experiments on six question-answering benchmarks demonstrate that MAPS consistently outperforms representative RAG methods across different backbone models. All code and resources are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/MAPS.

candidates.title: C$^2$U in RAG: Compositional Concept Unlearning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation can expose unwanted concepts through retrieved evidence even when the generator is moderated. We study query-side concept suppression with a fixed encoder and document index. Compositional Concept Unlearning (C$^2$U) routes a profile-derived direction through an augmented atom bank, adding only a bounded edited-minus-original delta to the raw query. Across five datasets, four encoders, and three seeds, the validation-selected configuration reduces pooled binary target Hit@5 by 4.25 percentage points with non-positive control degradation and target-exposure changes. Under the evaluated query transforms, it suppresses target density without increasing budgeted control-query exposure. Separately, ArXiv four-concept composition improves over an averaged-direction comparator after independent validation gates and first-use test evaluation.

candidates.title: NPUGen: NPU as KV Generator for Stable Long-Context Mobile LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: As on-device large language model (LLM) applications like mobile agents become increasingly popular, long-context inference has become a key challenge. The key-value (KV) cache is the foundation of efficient autoregressive decoding, but its memory footprint grows rapidly with context length, often exceeding the memory limits of mobile devices. Existing KV cache management methods, such as compression and storage offloading, often lead to performance degradation or unpredictable stall latency. We find that in the prevalent CPU/GPU-decoding mobile pipelines, the NPU remains largely idle during decoding and can recompute missing KV cache more efficiently than storage offloading. We therefore propose NPUGen, whose KV recomputation engine generates missing KV cache on the idle NPU via a prefill-like forward pass, avoiding unstable storage I/O, CPU intervention, and unnecessary data movement. NPUGen further introduces a hidden-state anchor mechanism that eliminates redundant prefix recomputation, and turns KV recomputation into a schedulable background service to cope with resource contention and guarantee foreground QoS. Experiments on smartphones with Qualcomm SoCs across multiple long-context tasks show that NPUGen significantly reduces decoding latency and fluctuations, providing fast and stable long-context inference on resource-constrained mobile devices.

candidates.title: Post-Training Weight Quantization in Small Language Models: Reasoning–Efficiency Trade-offs Across GGUF Precision Levels
candidates.abstract: Weight quantization can reduce the storage and computational requirements of languagemodels, but it may also affect their reasoning capabilities. This study investigates whetherquantization causes gradual or abrupt degradation in the reasoning performance of smalllanguage models. Three instruction-tuned models were evaluated: Qwen3-0.6B, Gemma 3 1BIT, Llama 3.2 1B Instruct. Each model was tested using a BF16 reference version and fiveGGUF quantization formats: Q8_0, Q6_K, Q5_K_M, Q4_K_M and Q3_K_M.Evaluation was performed on the same fixed 50-question subset of the GSM8K mathematicalreasoning dataset. Exact-answer accuracy, average latency, peak RAM usage, generationspeed, and stored model size were recorded. The results show that quantization did notproduce one universal degradation pattern. Accuracy changes varied across models andprecision levels. Qwen Q4_K_M matched its BF16 accuracy, Gemma Q4_K_M recorded a numerically higher accuracy than BF16 in this pilot sample, 44% versus 42%; this small difference should not beinterpreted as evidence of a meaningful improvement, and Llama Q6_K achieved the highest quantized accuracy for that model. However, Q3_K_M produced larger accuracy reductions for Qwen and Llama.Quantization consistently improved storage and inference efficiency. These findings suggestthat quantization provides practical efficiency benefits, but the effect on reasoningperformance is model-dependent.Keywords: weight quantization; small language models; GGUF; reasoning; llama.cpp;inference efficiency, GSM8K

candidates.title: Multimodal artificial intelligence and large language models in gastrointestinal endoscopy: From lesion detection to workflow-integrated report generation
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images.However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation.Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports.Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support.By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication.Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation.This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation.Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.

candidates.title: Experimental reasoning in large language models
candidates.abstract: Scientific reasoning requires interaction with the physical world: designing experiments, interpreting outcomes, and deciding what experiment should come next. Here we show that general-purpose large language models (LLMs) already possess substantial capabilities for experimental reasoning. We connected LLMs to a liquid-handling robot and camera through PEARL, which provides perception, action, and persistent state. Given objectives rather than prescribed workflows, the system designed and successfully executed experiments, interpreted observations, and revised its approach as evidence accumulated. When information was insufficient, PEARL autonomously designed and performed intermediate experiments to acquire it. In quantitative enzyme characterization, it judged whether measurements were sufficient, new data were required, or conditions needed to change. Across eight scenarios, these behaviors were reliable with limited agent scaffolding and no supplied scenario-specific recovery recipes. More broadly, general-purpose LLMs may provide a reasoning layer between scientific objectives and physical experimentation, shifting laboratory automation from executing predefined procedures toward AI systems that participate directly in the experimental process.

candidates.title: AI-Based Multimodal Phishing Detection Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Title: AI-Based Multimodal Phishing Detection Using Large Language Models Description: Phishing attacks are becoming increasingly sophisticated, making traditional detection techniques less effective against evolving cyber threats. This research proposes an AI-based multimodal phishing detection framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to analyze email content, URLs, and webpage-related features for identifying potential phishing attempts. The proposed framework aims to combine semantic understanding, URL analysis, and multimodal feature fusion to improve phishing detection, interpretability, and robustness. This paper reviews existing phishing detection techniques, identifies research gaps, and presents a conceptual architecture and evaluation methodology for future implementation and testing. candidates.title: Prism : Efficient Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning for On-Device LLMs
candidates.abstract: On-device fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) is becoming increasingly important for personalized AI assistants and adaptive agents. However, standard backpropagation imposes substantial training-state memory overheads that often exceed the stringent resource budgets of mobile platforms. To address this, Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization leverages forward-only probing instead of backpropagation, drastically reducing memory footprints and offering a compelling alternative for on-device adaptation. Nonetheless, scaling ZO fine-tuning to billion-scale trainable parameter spaces remains challenging, as the cost of recovering reliable update directions scales poorly with dimensionality under mobile constraints. In this paper, we present Prism, a mobile-native infrastructure for practical billion-scale on-device ZO fine-tuning. Prism re-architects the ZO loop around a scalable probing substrate, bringing both per-step training latency and memory overhead closer to the inference footprint. We implement Prism end to end on commodity smartphones and evaluate it across diverse tasks and multiple model scales. Prism achieves accuracy comparable to that of state-of-the-art ZO fine-tuning baselines while reducing per-step latency by 53.4%-76.3% and peak memory by 10.6%-13.8% relative to the best baseline in each setting. These results demonstrate the practical feasibility of billion-scale on-device ZO fine-tuning for LLMs under real mobile constraints. We will release our code to support future research.

candidates.title: Human Oversight for LLM-Assisted Clinical Documentation
candidates.abstract: Clinical documentation is essential to healthcare delivery but is timeconsuming, cognitively demanding, and prone to error. Large language models (LLMs) can generate draft notes, but may introduce hallucinations, unsupported inferences, or factual distortions that clinicians overlook. This study evaluated whether transparency features improve clinician oversight in LLM-assisted documentation. Using a crossover design, 40 clinicians reviewed AI-generated notes under three conditions: a standard LLM interface, token-level uncertainty highlighting, and uncertainty highlighting combined with direct links to electronic medical record fields. Outcomes included factual errors remaining in finalized notes, editing time, trust, perceived control, and cognitive load. The combined uncertainty-plus-source-link interface performed best, reducing factual errors by 41% and editing time by 18% compared with the standard condition. Uncertainty highlighting alone offered partial benefits but still required manual record verification. These findings indicate that LLM-assisted documentation is safer and more efficient when transparency features support verification, direct attention, and preserve clinician control.

candidates.title: HAWK: Heterogeneity-Aware KV Cache Transfer for Efficient GPU-NPU Phase-Disaggregated LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference exhibits distinct computational characteristics across its two phases: prefill is compute-intensive, whereas decode is more memory-bound. As a result, AI accelerators achieve varying levels of efficiency across the two phases. GPUs are well suited to prefill, but are often underutilized during decode. By contrast, NPUs can utilize their compute resources more effectively during decode. Motivated by this observation, we explore a heterogeneous architecture that integrates GPUs and NPUs, mapping prefill to GPUs and decode to NPUs to achieve high performance and efficiency. However, realizing such heterogeneous integration is challenging because LLM phase disaggregation requires KV cache transfer from prefill to decode (that is, from GPUs to NPUs), which is complicated by differences in inter-device communication mechanisms and KV cache tensor layouts. To address this, we propose HAWK, a transfer mechanism that enables rapid KV cache transfer across heterogeneous devices. HAWK establishes a remote direct memory access (RDMA) path for direct cross-device transfers while handling inter-device tensor layout discrepancies as part of the transfer process. In particular, HAWK allocates tensor-layout-aware RDMA buffers on the NPU side to match the target tensor layout. Leveraging these buffers, HAWK orchestrates data transfer from a conventional contiguous GPU RDMA buffer to the corresponding NPU buffers, allowing transferred tensors to be consumed directly without additional data rearrangement while maintaining transfer efficiency. We implement and evaluate HAWK on a system built with commercially available GPUs and NPUs, demonstrating performance within 7.88% of a GPU-only system under the same SLO constraints while achieving up to 1.26$\times$ higher power efficiency and 1.72$\times$ higher cost efficiency.

candidates.title: Networked trust-game data for "Does social networking agency shape trust and reciprocity similarly in large language model agents and humans?"
candidates.abstract: This dataset supports the manuscript “Does social networking agency shape trust and reciprocity similarly in large language model agents and humans?” The archive contains recorded decisions and generated responses from large language model (LLM) agents in a networked trust game, together with executed allocation tables, prompts, synthetic personas and archived experiment configurations. The main experiments comprise three sessions for each of five nominal proportions of free agents (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1). Each session includes 49 agents on a periodic 7 × 7 lattice with four neighbours and lasts 20 rounds. Each agent acts as both trustor and trustee in each round. Free trustors may differentiate investments across neighbours, whereas constrained trustors allocate equally. The three CSV exports contain 14,700 agent-round records in total. A separate exploratory dataset contains one 20-round session per nominal proportion. These sessions used a different instruction concerning terminal-round assumptions and should not be pooled with the main experiments as repetitions of the same protocol. The included README provides the directory structure, experimental conditions, JSON schema, CSV data dictionary and guidance for reuse. Behavioural analyses of the main experiments should use the executed allocations rather than assume that allocations stated in generated text were executed unchanged. Amounts and payoffs are expressed in experimental tokens, not currency. Human benchmark data are not included. They originate from Jia et al. (2025), “Social networking agency and prosociality are inextricably linked in economic games” (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02289-0), and are available from the original authors’ project at https://osf.io/n84dv/. candidates.title: HalluciGuard-eye: knowledge graph-enhanced retrieval-augmented generation for hallucination detection and mitigation in ophthalmic multimodal large language models
candidates.abstract: Background Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults, yet scalable early detection is limited by the unreliability of AI-assisted screening. Multimodal large language models can interpret fundus photographs and support DR grading, but they frequently hallucinate - fabricating lesions or misclassifying referable DR - which directly threatens timely treatment and prevention of vision loss. We developed HalluciGuard-Eye to make AI-assisted DR assessment trustworthy. Methods HalluciGuard-Eye combines knowledge graph-enhanced retrieval-augmented generation with hierarchical hallucination detection. An Ophthalmic Clinical Knowledge Graph containing 47,832 medical entities and 156,294 semantic relationships was constructed from clinical guidelines and published literature. A dual-stream architecture uses a Visual-Semantic Alignment Module to verify cross-modal consistency and a Clinical Factuality Grounding Network to anchor generated content to reranked evidence. The Hierarchical Factuality Score assesses anatomical, pathological, and clinical-recommendation accuracy. The framework was evaluated on four public ophthalmic imaging benchmarks. Results HalluciGuard-Eye reduced hallucination rates by 42.2% compared with state-of-the-art medical multimodal large language models and achieved 91.6% factual accuracy for clinical entity recognition on EyePACS. For diabetic retinopathy grading, sensitivity was 89.6% and specificity was 92.1%, representing improvements of 2.4% and 2.7%, respectively, over MedRAG. In the component ablation, removing knowledge-graph retrieval lowered EyePACS HFS by 9.4 percentage points. Additional analyses yielded 87.6% critical-evidence recall@20, 89.2% lesion-location accuracy, and 88.9% sensitivity in a patient-clustered cohort. Conclusions These results indicate that knowledge-grounded retrieval and hierarchical factuality assessment can reduce hallucinations while preserving diagnostic performance in ophthalmic multimodal language models.

candidates.title: Comparative Analysis of Transformer Models for Prompt Injection Detection in Autonomous Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Prompt injection attacks pose a significant security challenge for large language model systems, particularly autonomous large language model-based agents that may interact with external tools, application programming interfaces, and data sources.This study presents a comparative evaluation of five pre-trained transformer models, namely BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, DistilBERT, and ALBERT, fine-tuned for binary prompt injection classification.A balanced dataset of 4,224 samples was compiled from 10 publicly accessible corpora containing benign and injection prompts and divided into training (2,956), validation (634), and test (634) sets.The models were trained in the Kaggle environment using an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, the AdamW optimizer, and a linear warm-up scheduling strategy.On the held-out test set, RoBERTa achieved the highest classification performance, with 97.48% accuracy, 97.52% macro-precision, 97.48% macro-recall, 97.48% macro-F1-score, and 99.64% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.DistilBERT achieved the highest reported throughput of 819.13 samples/s and the lowest per-sample latency of 1.22 ms.Statistical analysis using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and SHapley Additive exPlanations-based interpretability analysis were also conducted to examine model differences and influential linguistic features.The findings demonstrate that fine-tuned transformer classifiers can achieve strong performance on the evaluated benchmark dataset while exhibiting different accuracyefficiency characteristics.However, the results should be interpreted within the scope of the evaluated data distribution, as the study does not include independent external datasets or adaptive adversarial attacks.These limitations indicate that further validation is required to establish generalizability and robustness in real-world prompt-injection defense scenarios.

candidates.title: Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over Federated Cloud Data Lakes
candidates.abstract: Abstract: Enterprise deployments of large language models require grounding generated answers in authoritative, continuously updated internal repositories while strictly enforcing row- and document-level access control lists (ACLs). Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines that chunk PDF documents into fixed 500-token windows and execute unconstrained approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) vector searches fail in production across three dimensions: they lose cross-section structural context in complex financial and technical tables, they suffer lexical blindness on exact product codes and regulatory statutes, and they leak unauthorized knowledge when ACL filtering is applied post-retrieval. This paper presents a federated Enterprise RAG architecture spanning cloud data lakes (Apache Iceberg on AWS S3, Snowflake, and Google BigQuery). Building on foundational RAG formulations (Lewis et al., 2020), ColBERT late-interaction retrieval (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020), and GraphRAG hierarchical community indexing (Edge et al., 2024), our architecture combines layout-aware semantic chunking, contextual header injection, three-way hybrid retrieval (dense HNSW vectors + BM25s sparse lexical + entity knowledge graph traversal) fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al., 2009), cross-encoder reranking, and cryptographic pre-retrieval ACL bitmap filtering. We evaluate the architecture through a production case study modeled on Morgan Stanley Wealth Management knowledge assistants and Ramp automated financial document analysis pipelines over a 14.8-million-document federated corpus. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that hybrid ACL-aware RAG increases Context Recall@10 from 61.2% (dense-only baseline) to 93.4%, raises RAGAS Faithfulness from 0.74 to 0.96, reduces hallucinated ungrounded claims from 14.8% to 1.2%, and enforces zero unauthorized document leakage at a P95 end-to-end retrieval latency of 168 milliseconds. Research Domain & Specialization Track Master of Science in Information Technology (MSIT) — Information Retrieval, Enterprise Generative AI, and Cloud Data Lakes. Core Technical Highlights Empirical Production Case Studies: Rigorous architectural blueprints and telemetry evaluation across enterprise cloud deployments. Four-Tier Reference Architecture: Formal specification from edge ingress to distributed hardware execution pools. Mathematical Formulation: Formally derived algorithmic and optimization models with closed-loop verification. Multi-Modal Benchmarking: Comparative empirical baselines under fault-injection and synthetic workload scaling. candidates.title: A Zero-Shot Multimodal Agent Framework for Power Line Inspection via Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: With the widespread deployment of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in smart grids, visual inspection based on deep learning has significantly advanced. However, conventional object detection paradigms heavily rely on massive, high-quality annotated datasets, struggling with poor generalization and a fundamental “data-hungry” dilemma caused by the extreme scarcity of long-tail defect samples. To overcome these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel zero-shot multimodal agent framework driven by large language models (LLMs). Adopting a centralized star topology, the architecture strictly decouples physical visual perception from high-level business cognition, utilizing an LLM as the cognitive hub and a vision-language model (VLM) as the perception tool. Crucially, the system introduces a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanism to dynamically align visual findings with authoritative grid regulations, supporting rule-referenced report generation. Experimental results demonstrate that, without any domain-specific fine-tuning, the proposed framework reduces false alarms under the tested configuration, with a detection F1 score of 82.52%. In a common-report comparison repeated three times, the framework achieves 65.30% correct reference-clause coverage, compared with 43.84% for a direct Qwen-VL-Max call supplied with the same visual priors and rules. The framework extends visual detection to structured, human-readable reports linked to supplied industrial rules; its grading accuracy and repeatability remain dependent on the visual observations and subsequent tool execution.

candidates.title: Sistem Tanya Jawab Resep Nusantara Berbasis Qwen dan Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Pengembangan sistem question answering pada domain resep masakan menghadapi tantangan dalam menghasilkan jawaban yang koheren secara bahasa sekaligus konsisten terhadap bahan, langkah memasak, dan konteks prosedural dokumen sumber. Large Language Model (LLM) seperti Qwen memiliki kemampuan memahami dan menghasilkan teks, namun berpotensi menghasilkan hallucination ketika jawaban tidak didukung informasi relevan. Penelitian ini mengembangkan sistem tanya jawab resep masakan Nusantara berbasis Qwen dan Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) untuk meningkatkan relevansi dan groundedness jawaban terhadap knowledge base resep. Dataset yang digunakan berasal dari Indonesian Food Recipes Dataset, diproses melalui tahap preprocessing, pembentukan data question-answer, fine-tuning model, dan pembangunan sistem retrieval berbasis vector database. Evaluasi dilakukan menggunakan metrik ROUGE, Recall@K, Grounded ROUGE, Grounded Ingredient Coverage, Answered Rate, dan No-answer Rate. Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan bahwa integrasi RAG meningkatkan kualitas dan keterikatan jawaban dibandingkan model tanpa retrieval, dengan performa terbaik diperoleh oleh skenario RAG + Fine-tuned Qwen yang mencapai ROUGE-L sebesar 0.413, Grounded ROUGE-L sebesar 0.926, dan Grounded Ingredient Coverage sebesar 0.967. Mekanisme tambahan yang dikonfigurasi pada sistem, yaitu no-answer filtering dan fallback retrieval, juga membantu menjaga konsistensi jawaban ketika konteks retrieval yang diperoleh kurang relevan. Penelitian ini diharapkan dapat menjadi langkah awal dalam pengembangan sistem question answering domain-spesifik berbasis LLM yang lebih konsisten dan grounded, khususnya pada pengetahuan prosedural seperti resep masakan Nusantara.

candidates.title: Projected-Feature Scale Calibration for 2-Bit Vision Encoders in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Very low-bit quantization of a multimodal large language model’s vision encoder can impair text recognition and chart understanding. We present projected-feature scale calibration (PSC), an image-only post-training method for 2-bit vision encoders. PSC starts from range-searched GPTQ, fixes integer codes and zero points, and jointly updates existing group scales by matching features through a frozen multimodal projector. This objective aligns image-only calibration with the visual representation supplied to the language model. The learned updates fold directly into the original scales, preserving the inference architecture. Experiments on LLaVA-OneVision show consistent improvements in text recognition and chart understanding over the same strong quantized initialization, including under simultaneous language-model compression. Matched controls support projected-feature supervision over encoder-output reconstruction, repeated calibration samples confirm stable gains, and an unchanged-recipe contrastive language–image pre-training (CLIP) evaluation supports transfer to a second encoder. PSC thus improves the accuracy of compact vision encoders while preserving their quantized representation.

candidates.title: Adaptive Stopping of Streamed Reasoning for Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Reasoning-enabled language model agents can incur substantial computation before acting, although the reasoning needed varies across decisions. Existing stopping signals, such as confidence and intermediate-answer stability, can vary in effectiveness across reasoning models; signals obtained from hidden states or token probabilities also require internal access that may be unavailable or impractical. We introduce StreamStop, which learns model-specific stopping policies offline from prefix-level action agreement. A frozen prefix reader encodes available reasoning text for a lightweight stop head, allowing stopping without access to the reasoning model's internal signals. We construct and publicly release a dataset of agent reasoning trajectories with prefix-level action annotations. These annotations compare each prefix action with the full-reasoning reference action, enabling offline comparison of stopping rules and exact expected-return optimization of a discounted action-agreement objective. Conditioning the head on the discount factor allows the agreement-token trade-off to be adjusted at inference without retraining. In closed-loop evaluations on WebShop and ScienceWorld, StreamStop achieves higher observed success than most validation-selected fixed-budget settings while using fewer reasoning tokens than Full thinking. On WebShop with Qwen3.8-27B, it uses 42% fewer reasoning tokens per episode with similar observed task success.

candidates.title: Agentic Ensemble with Vision-Language Models for Visual Anomaly Detection
candidates.abstract: Visual anomaly detection aims to detect abnormal objects, while anomaly samples are often scarce during model training. Assembling multiple pretrained detectors can help by leveraging their transferable image scores and anomaly maps. However, most existing ensemble methods apply fixed fusion rules over saved predictions which struggle when pretrained detectors clearly disagree due to different training objectives, priors, and visual representations. To this end, we design AnomalyAgent, a post-training fusion framework for accurate visual anomaly detection. AnomalyAgent aligns heterogeneous scores and maps, summarizes score- and region-level disagreement, and treats fusion as a finite action-selection problem. It implements two types of actions: 1) score actions that determine how to fuse image-level detector confidence via consensus, robust aggregation, detector weighting, or score-map consistency; 2) map actions that fuse dense anomaly responses via consensus, detector weighting, geometric aggregation, or disagreement correction. A constrained vision-language model (VLM) is introduced to inspect high-conflict samples and select valid score action and map action to produce the final prediction. We evaluate AnomalyAgent on MVTec AD and VisA as primary benchmarks, together with seven additional public anomaly benchmarks and Real-IAD for large-scale score-level evaluation. Across these benchmarks, AnomalyAgent consistently improves over equal-weight fusion and achieves the best mean image AUROC and pixel AP among the compared fusion methods on MVTec AD and VisA, while demonstrating robust transfer across additional anomaly domains.

candidates.title: Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Tactile Multimodal Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Tactile Perception, Reasoning, Generation, and Physical Feedback
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have expanded artificial intelligence beyond text to include visual and auditory information. However, tactile interaction remains comparatively fragmented across sensing hardware, haptic signal interpretation, tactile generation, and device-specific feedback mechanisms. This paper proposes Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Tactile Multimodal Intelligence (SBTMI), a conceptual framework for integrating tactile input and physical tactile output into smartphone-centered multimodal large language model systems. Unlike approaches that focus exclusively on tactile classification, tactile captioning, or the generation of haptic effects from textual descriptions, the proposed framework organizes tactile perception, semantic reasoning, tactile generation, physical actuation, and feedback-based adaptation within a unified interaction architecture. The framework consists of five principal components: a tactile acquisition interface, a tactile representation module, a multimodal reasoning controller, a tactile generation module, and a device-specific actuation interface. A closed-loop interaction mechanism enables the system to compare intended tactile effects with subsequent sensor observations and adjust its outputs accordingly. The framework distinguishes native smartphone capabilities from capabilities requiring external tactile sensors or actuators. We formulate research questions, define optimization objectives and evaluation metrics, and propose experiments for assessing tactile understanding, generation quality, cross-modal consistency, latency, robustness, and closed-loop performance. This work is a conceptual research proposal rather than an empirically validated system. Its contribution is a unified architectural and experimental framework for investigating bidirectional tactile intelligence in smartphone-centered multimodal AI.

candidates.title: Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Pain-Related Multimodal Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Pain Sensing, Contextual Reasoning, Safe Sensory Feedback, and Adaptive Interaction
candidates.abstract: Pain is a complex sensory and affective experience that is difficult to measure objectively and cannot be reduced to a single physiological signal. Smartphones and wearable devices have already been used to collect pain reports, monitor physiological correlates, and support pain assessment. Separately, artificial nociceptive systems and sensory-feedback interfaces have investigated how machines can detect potentially harmful stimuli and communicate information through physical feedback. However, the integration of pain-related sensing, multimodal large language model reasoning, and safe, bidirectional sensory interaction within a smartphone-centered architecture remains a research question requiring systematic investigation. This paper proposes Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Pain-Related Multimodal Large Language Models (SBP-MLLMs), a conceptual framework for integrating pain-related input and controlled sensory feedback with multimodal reasoning. The architecture includes a smartphone host, a pain-related data acquisition interface, a multimodal representation encoder, a contextual reasoning controller, a safety-constrained feedback planner, and an output interface. The input pathway combines voluntary pain reports with available physiological, behavioral, and contextual information, while explicitly distinguishing measured signals from subjective pain experience. The output pathway communicates pain-related information through visual, auditory, vibrotactile, or other validated non-injurious feedback. Where clinically justified, specialized external devices may be considered under appropriate professional oversight, but the proposed framework does not require deliberately inducing pain. A closed-loop controller compares intended feedback with observed user responses and device status, while respecting consent and safety constraints. The paper formalizes the architecture, identifies research questions, and proposes an experimental evaluation protocol. The framework is conceptual and has not been experimentally validated. Its potential contribution is the integration of pain-related perception, multimodal reasoning, and safe bidirectional interaction rather than the invention of pain sensing, pain monitoring, or sensory stimulation.

candidates.title: Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Olfactory Multimodal Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Smell Sensing, Semantic Reasoning, Scent Generation, and Closed-Loop Olfactory Interaction
candidates.abstract: Human–computer interaction has primarily relied on visual, auditory, and tactile channels, while olfaction remains comparatively underrepresented in general-purpose mobile computing. Recent advances in electronic noses, smartphone-connected gas sensors, artificial intelligence-based scent creation, and wearable olfactory displays provide important foundations for integrating smell into digital systems. However, a unified architecture in which a smartphone-centered multimodal large language model coordinates olfactory input, semantic interpretation, context-dependent scent generation, and feedback-based correction remains a research direction requiring systematic investigation. This paper proposes Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Olfactory Multimodal Large Language Models (SBOM-LLMs), a conceptual framework that integrates olfactory sensing and physical scent output with multimodal large language model reasoning. The proposed architecture consists of six components: a smartphone host, an olfactory acquisition interface, an olfactory representation encoder, a multimodal reasoning controller, a constrained scent-generation planner, and a physical olfactory output interface. The framework supports two complementary capabilities: translating environmental odor measurements into machine-interpretable semantic representations and translating multimodal intentions into controlled physical scent outputs. A closed-loop mechanism compares intended scent specifications with sensor measurements and available delivery telemetry, enabling iterative adjustment when appropriate. The paper formalizes the architecture, defines candidate optimization objectives, proposes an experimental evaluation protocol, and discusses safety, calibration, personalization, and hardware constraints. This work presents a conceptual research framework rather than a validated implementation. Its potential contribution lies in the integration and coordination of existing olfactory technologies with general-purpose multimodal reasoning, not in claiming to invent electronic noses or digital scent displays.

candidates.title: Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Gustatory Multimodal Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Taste Sensing, Reasoning, Generation, and Physical Taste Feedback
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly integrate text, images, and audio, yet taste remains an underrepresented modality in smartphone-centered artificial intelligence. Existing research has developed electronic tongues, portable taste interfaces, digital taste stimulation, and sensor–actuator systems for remote tasting. However, the integration of these capabilities into a unified smartphone-centered multimodal large language model presents additional research questions concerning sensory representation, semantic reasoning, taste generation, device control, and feedback-based adaptation. This paper proposes Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Gustatory Intelligence (SNBGI), a conceptual framework that connects gustatory input and gustatory output through a common multimodal reasoning architecture. The proposed system receives taste-related chemical measurements from electronic-tongue sensors or compatible sensing peripherals, interprets these observations in context, generates structured gustatory output specifications, and communicates with a device capable of producing controlled taste stimuli. A closed-loop mechanism enables the system to compare intended taste profiles with subsequent sensor measurements and user feedback. The framework distinguishes objective chemical sensing from subjective human taste perception and distinguishes smartphone software from the external hardware required for physical taste stimulation. We formulate research questions, mathematical objectives, implementation components, and an experimental protocol for evaluating taste classification, generation accuracy, perceptual correspondence, response latency, portability, and safety. The contribution is a proposed architecture and validation program, not a claim that digital taste sensing or generation has been invented for the first time. The framework aims to provide a foundation for investigating how smartphone-based multimodal AI can perceive, reason about, and generate taste-related experiences.

candidates.title: PI-MLLM: Psychophysics-Inspired Multimodal Large Language Model for Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis
candidates.abstract: Oddly Satisfying Videos (OSVs) can evoke strong viewer responses through repetitive motion, visual tactility, and ASMR-like sounds despite containing few explicit semantic emotion cues. This makes OSVs a challenging setting for Video Emotion Analysis (VEA), since most existing methods focus on semantic video content and under-model the physical sensory dynamics that shape viewer responses. To support Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis (OSVEA), we construct the Oddly Satisfying Video Dataset (OSVD), comprising 12,000 annotated 5-second clips. Each clip provides viewer-emotion labels under video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual conditions, together with explanations grounded in visual and acoustic sensory evidence. Building on OSVD, we propose PI-MLLM, a psychophysics-inspired multimodal large language model that integrates Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment (MSDA) and Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution (CAVA). MSDA uses auxiliary prediction objectives to align modality representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics. CAVA evaluates emotion scores across modality coalitions and applies Shapley attribution to identify the dominant modality and determine whether visual and auditory evidence is synergistic or conflicting. Experiments show that PI-MLLM improves both viewer-side emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality, suggesting the value of physical sensory cues to video emotion analysis.

candidates.title: Imagination or Reason? A Spinozist Criterion for Genuine Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: When Webb, Holyoak, and Lu reported that large language models (LLMs) solve a wide range of analogy problems zero-shot, they reopened an old philosophical question: do such systems reason relationally, or do they exploit surface regularities absorbed from training? Critics show that performance degrades on counterfactual variants that leave human performance intact; defenders answer that these failures reflect peripheral deficits. I argue that the debate lacks a principled criterion for distinguishing genuine relational reasoning from associative pattern-completion, and that Spinoza’s epistemology supplies one. Spinoza separates imagination—general ideas formed through the contingent order in which the body is affected—from reason, the adequate cognition of what is genuinely common through common notions; his own illustration (Ethics 2p40s2) is a proportional analogy that turns on the difference between applying a learned rule and grasping a common form. Reconstructed functionally, the distinction yields a diagnostic heuristic: invariance of competence under transformations that preserve relational structure while destroying surface similarity counts as defeasible evidence of relational grounding. This separates the following two questions the literature conflates: whether a system produces correct analogies, and whether its competence is relationally grounded. I give the criterion a measurement protocol and apply it symmetrically to humans and machines.

candidates.title: Hidden Messages Between Diffusion Language Model Agents: Causal Evidence for Latent Communication
candidates.abstract: Diffusion language models form answers through a sequence of revisable continuous states, but multi-agent systems usually discard those states and make agents communicate only after decoding text. We ask whether one independent diffusion trajectory can pass a compact hidden message into another and, crucially, whether the receiver uses what that message means. In Hidden Messages, a sender compresses its denoising state into four signed dense vectors; the receiver consumes them while retaining its own context, canvas, and trajectory. Removing a message tests whether the channel matters; replacing it with a message from another example tests whether its content matters. Across controlled tasks, derangement removes a +63.6-point advantage on Tiny-A2D and a +100.0-point advantage on Dream-7B, while targeted substitutions steer the receiver toward the substituted fact. On QASC with the two supporting facts split across agents, matched communication reaches 80.8%, but a wrong-example message lowers accuracy to 46.8%, a content effect of +34.0 points. The surprising result is temporal: one late transfer reaches 87.8%, exceeding four recurrent exchanges by +7.0 points. These experiments provide causal evidence for continuous hidden communication between diffusion-LM agents and show that when information is transferred can matter more than how many times agents exchange it.

candidates.title: Fundamentals of Natural Language Processing and Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: This chapter introduces the fundamental principles of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models (LLMs) within the context of Sports Science and data-driven analytics. It demonstrates how unstructured textual and vocal data complement traditional numerical performance metrics by capturing contextual, psychological, and communicative aspects of sport environments. The chapter systematically presents core NLP techniques, including tokenization, lemmatization, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, topic modeling, and word embeddings, and explains their role in transforming language-based data into structured representations for performance analysis and decision-making. Building on these foundations, the chapter examines key neural network architectures used in NLP, particularly recurrent neural networks, Long Short-Term Memory models, and Transformer-based systems. Special emphasis is placed on the attention mechanism and its role in enabling scalable and context-aware language modelling. The chapter further analyzes the capabilities and limitations of Large Language Models, including their generative potential, adaptability through fine-tuning and prompt-based interaction, and challenges such as hallucinations, bias, and interpretability. Through multimodal integration and applied case studies, the chapter highlights how NLP and LLMs contribute to sports analytics, athlete monitoring, talent identification, and real-time decision-making.
