candidates.title: Comparing BM25, Multilingual-E5, and Reciprocal Rank Fusion for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) incorporates externally retrieved information as contextual knowledge to improve the quality of responses generated by language models. However, a RAG system's effectiveness depends heavily on the retrieval method's ability to identify and rank relevant documents. This study compares BM25, Multilingual-E5, and a hybrid approach based on Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) using a product and service catalog corpus consisting of 145 documents and 40 benchmark queries. The evaluation was conducted in two stages: retrieval performance was assessed using Hit@1, Hit@3, Hit@5, and MRR@5, while RAG answer quality was evaluated using Faithfulness, Answer Relevancy, and Answer Accuracy. The results show that BM25 achieved the highest Hit@1 score (0.775) and MRR@5 (0.8279), whereas Multilingual-E5 achieved the highest Hit@5 score (0.950). For answer quality, Multilingual-E5 obtained the highest Faithfulness score (0.9667), while the hybrid RRF approach achieved the highest Answer Relevancy score (0.8451); both achieved an Answer Accuracy score (0.7938). Statistical tests revealed no significant differences among the retrieval methods. Answer Relevancy and Answer Accuracy were descriptively lower when the target document was absent from the Top-5 context, whereas the target's exact position within ranks 1-5 showed no significant correlation with answer quality. A context-size robustness analysis further showed descriptive improvements in Answer Relevancy and Answer Accuracy from Top-1 to Top-3 and Top-5, although none of the nine context-size effects remained statistically significant after Holm correction. Under a criterion emphasizing Top-5 target coverage and downstream answer quality, Multilingual-E5 showed a favorable operational profile under the evaluated configuration.

candidates.title: "FAQGenie: An Intelligent FAQ Assistant Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation"
candidates.abstract: "Dataset Description\u2014Vedranta Bank Synthetic Banking Document DatasetThe Vedranta Bank Synthetic Banking Document Dataset is a collection of artificially generated PDF documents representing the policies, services, procedures, and operational information of a fictional financial institution. The dataset is designed to support the development, testing, and evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems in the banking domain. It provides a controlled knowledge base for evaluating document parsing, text chunking, semantic embedding, vector-based similarity search, contextual retrieval, and grounded response generation. The documents simulate banking-related information and enable testing of question-answering systems across multiple categories of customer and operational queries. By using synthetic rather than real banking records, the dataset avoids dependence on confidential customer information while supporting reproducible experimentation. It can be integrated with embedding models and vector databases to assess retrieval relevance, answer accuracy, contextual grounding, and source attribution. The dataset is intended for academic research, educational projects, and prototyping of document-grounded conversational assistants. As the documents are synthetic and represent a fictional bank, the dataset does not constitute authentic financial documentation and should not be used for real banking decisions."

candidates.title: VisConf: Quality-Aware Consensus for Best-of-N in Vision-Language Model Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Best-of-N methods improve text-only LLM reasoning by sampling multiple trajectories before selecting an answer. For Vision-Language Models (VLMs), answer frequency and model confidence alone can be insufficient, as sampled generations also vary in their engagement with the visual input. We find that distributional confidence and visual attention are complementary indicators of rollout quality. Each is limited on its own, while trajectories that show strong signals in both are more likely to be correct. Motivated by this, we introduce VisConf, a rollout-quality score that multiplicatively combines visual engagement with candidate-calibrated Self-Certainty, penalizing rollouts that are weak in either signal. We incorporate Rank-Weighted Consensus (RWC), a tuning-free aggregation rule that converts within-question VisConf ranks into answer-level vote weights. Across three VLMs on MathVista, MMMU-Pro, and MMStar, VisConf with RWC consistently outperforms strong BoN baselines. Our analysis shows particularly large gains when correct trajectories are present but underrepresented in the candidate pool.

candidates.title: Characterising and Analysing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Techniques
candidates.abstract: The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) across many application domains has increased the need for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM performance. Thus far, several RAG techniques with impressive features and capabilities have been proposed in the literature, making it a herculean task to select the most appropriate RAG techniques for specific problem scenarios. Thus, we propose a conceptual framework comprising main dimensions and sub-dimensions for characterising (defining "what it is") and analysing (defining "how well it does") existing RAG techniques. The conceptual framework was developed through a qualitative analysis of the attributes of RAG techniques reported in the literature. It can serve as a pre-empirical filtering mechanism for researchers and practitioners in selecting the highest-fit RAG candidates that meet specific user and task requirements before empirical benchmarking of RAG techniques, which can be computationally and financially expensive.

candidates.title: On the Position Bias of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Study
candidates.abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability.

candidates.title: Who Pays for Efficient Inference? Confidence-Based Small-to-Large LLM Routing Across Tasks and Languages
candidates.abstract: Small-to-large language model routing can reduce inference cost by escalating difficult inputs while retaining easier ones on a smaller model. Its success, however, depends on identifying examples that benefit from escalation, and the reliability of confidence across multilingual tasks remains unclear. We present a systematic evaluation of confidence-based routing across three model families, four languages, and three task types, covering 72 model, dataset, language, and scale configurations and 42,288 predictions. We compare global confidence routing with random routing, equal-quota confidence routing, and an oracle upper bound. Confidence identifies beneficial escalations on the Belebele reading comprehension and SIB-200 topic classification datasets, with mean correction-detection AUCs of 0.612 and 0.705. At 50% escalation, it improves over random routing by 1.40--4.67 percentage points on Belebele and 2.54--5.63 points on SIB-200. In contrast, the mean AUC on the MMLU-ProX-Lite knowledge and reasoning dataset is only 0.510, and routing provides no consistent improvement over random selection because small models often remain highly confident while incorrect. Global confidence routing also creates language escalation gaps up to 30.33 percentage points, whereas equal-quota routing removes this disparity with little aggregate accuracy cost. These results show that confidence routing is task-dependent and can allocate computation unevenly across languages. Code is available at https://github.com/sabbir5622r/multilingual-llm-routing

candidates.title: Under the Skin: Backdoor Infection in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in generating text conditioned on inputs from different modalities. In this work, we introduce backdoor infection, a cross-modal attack framework targeting MLLMs. Starting from a model already injected with a backdoor in one modality, our attack constructs a corresponding trigger in another modality, called the infected modality. Exploiting the model's shared latent space, the trigger in the infected modality reliably activates the malicious behavior, without modifying or poisoning the infected modality during training. We further develop a lightweight, constraint-aware optimization method for efficient and practical trigger generation. Extensive experiments across several state-of-the-art MLLMs, including LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen-VL, and Gemma, demonstrate that our approach identifies cross-modal triggers that are more efficient, effective, and less detectable than direct optimization baselines, highlighting a critical new threat vector in multimodal systems.

candidates.title: Competence-Based Evaluation of Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. Such a performance-based evaluation methodology says little about a model's generalization capacity in reasoning. To address this limitation, we argue for a different evaluation paradigm, called competence-based evaluation (CBE), which tests whether models reliably apply the same competence across a family of problems. A parameterized generator scales complexity while keeping the required competence fixed, and matched answer-preserving presentations test correctness beyond one formulation. We instantiate CBE on elementary ordering tasks, scaling input size while varying presentations of the same ordering rule. Across six GPT and Qwen models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family. Chain-of-thought and GRPO extend strong performance without resolving all tested failures; supervised LoRA shows little held-out transfer. CBE provides diagnostic profiles and an evaluation protocol that can grow with future models.

candidates.title: A Comparative Analysis of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering, summarisation, coding, and research support, yet choosing a suitable model remains difficult because models differ in performance, context capacity, cost, privacy, and deployment options. This paper presents a document-based comparative analysis of five LLMs: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 405B Instruct, and Mistral Large 2. Using published technical reports, official documentation, model cards, and recognised benchmark studies, the models are examined under a common framework covering response quality, reasoning, coding, language understanding, context-window capacity, speed, computational requirements, cost, privacy, and deployment flexibility. No new experiments are conducted, and results obtained under different evaluation conditions are not treated as directly equivalent. The analysis shows that model selection involves trade-offs: hosted models offer easier access, whereas models with downloadable weights give greater deployment control but require more computing resources. No single model is found to be best for every task, which supports a task-specific approach to selecting LLMs.

candidates.title: Prism Attention: Proposal-Refined Index Sharing Mechanism for Efficient LLMs Inference
candidates.abstract: Long-context decoding in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory and computation required to attend over an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache at each autoregressive step. Although token-level sparse attention reduces this burden by restricting computation to a small subset of relevant past tokens, its practical gains are often offset by repeatedly recomputing layer-wise sparse indices as the context grows. A common remedy is to share sparse indices across layers by computing them only at designated anchor layers, but such static reuse ignores the layer-wise evolution of attention patterns, causing the reused indices to progressively deviate from the layer-specific optima and incur substantial attention loss. By revisiting cross-layer sparsity from the perspective of attention dynamics, we find that inter-layer salient token shift is highly localized: although the exact top-$κ$ indices differ across layers, the core high-attention tokens remain stable, with changes concentrated near the expanded boundary of previously selected regions. Motivated by this, we propose Prism Attention, a proposal-refined sparse attention framework. It replaces rigid cross-layer index reuse with a coarse-to-fine strategy, preserving layer-wise adaptability while retaining the efficiency benefits of cross-layer sharing. Extensive experiments show that Prism Attention achieves state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse attention methods on both reasoning and long-context benchmarks, while attaining a $3.4\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context length.

candidates.title: FLARE: Physics-Grounded Evaluation of Language-Model Agents for Feeder Restoration with Degraded Observations
candidates.abstract: Restoring service after distribution-grid faults requires decisions from incomplete and conflicting information while respecting electrical constraints. Addressing this need, we introduce FLARE (Feeder-Level Agent Restoration Evaluation), a physics-grounded benchmark for post-isolation feeder restoration. FLARE con- tains 800 AC-feasible cases across five observation settings and allows agents to gather evidence, evaluate switches, and perform restoration actions under fixed operational limits. We evaluate five instruction-tuned models over 78,750 episodes, including topology, distributed-generation, and loading shifts. Mean normalized regret ranges from 0.082 to 0.148. Although every model has zero median regret, P95 regret ranges from 0.814 to 1.000, revealing an important failure tail. Shadow replay shows that 96.4% of 15,706 guard-rejected actions would have caused a physical violation. FLARE enables reproducible evaluation of language-model based restoration support while emphasizing the need for external safety checks.

candidates.title: Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Tree Search
candidates.abstract: Tree search enhances multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet prevailing methods expand every step with a fixed budget, irrespective of the marginal utility of expansion. We first show, across existing search algorithms, that continuations sampled from a shared intermediate state are largely duplicates and collapse to a few distinct answers. Critically, we find that the semantic dispersion of sibling actions predicts the redundancy of their downstream continuations, permitting a subtree's budget to be fixed before expansion. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this: treating the per-step budget as the Monte Carlo sample size for estimating a step's residual answer entropy, we derive a sufficient budget that shrinks with sibling dispersion. We accordingly propose $\textbf{Uncertainty-Aware Allocation}$ (UAA), a training-free framework that decouples value from uncertainty: values determine which candidates are promising, while uncertainty, estimated from sibling dispersion at no additional model cost, determines how many merit expansion, via uncertainty-aware pruning and uncertainty-aware budgeting. Across mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token usage by up to $90\%$ and latency by up to $9\times$ at comparable accuracy, generalizing across four tree search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.

candidates.title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.

candidates.title: KiranaBench: Can a Language Model Run a Neighbourhood Shop?
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on long-horizon tasks, including autonomously running a business. Existing benchmarks for this setting are almost exclusively English-language, Western in retail context, and single-agent, with the agent observing the business directly. We study how these results transfer to a multi-agent Indic setting. We introduce KiranaBench, a simulated Indian general store in which four roles (manager, cashier, helper, and bookkeeper) are each played by a separate LLM agent. Interactions with customers and suppliers occur in English, Hindi, or Hinglish, and product demand is calibrated to India's national Household Consumption Expenditure Survey. Evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that all fall far short of a fixed-rule shopkeeper baseline: the best model earns only one-eighth of the baseline's profit, and two models finish below an unmanaged shop. Performance is also consistently lower for Hindi and Hinglish than for English supplier communication. KiranaBench offers evidence that current LLM agents are not yet reliable for autonomously operating small businesses in India, and provides a testbed for developing agents suited to settings that are long-horizon, collaborative, and multilingual.

candidates.title: Efficient and Effective Test Generation and Type Inference for Python Applications
candidates.abstract: Python has become one of the most widely used programming languages, valued for its flexibility and ease of use. However, its dynamic nature provides only limited static guarantees, making programs more difficult to write reliably: errors are more likely to remain undetected until runtime. Tests and type checking can mitigate these issues by detecting bugs—including runtime errors—before release, but creating tests and the type annotations required for checking demands substantial developer effort, discouraging their widespread use. Approaches to automating test generation and type inference are hindered not only by Python’s dynamic features but also by the substantial performance limitations of CPython, the standard Python interpreter, which make dynamic analysis costly in practice. In this dissertation, I explore how low-overhead dynamic analysis can be used to improve the reliability of Python software. First, I introduce SlipCover, a code coverage measurement tool that significantly reduces runtime overhead through efficient bytecode instrumentation and dynamic de-instrumentation. SlipCover enables practical use of coverage tracking in iterative workflows by achieving near-zero overhead, supporting a range of software engineering applications. Building on SlipCover, I next present CoverUp, a regression test generation tool that uses coverage feedback to efficiently guide a large language model in generating unit tests that significantly outperform previous methods in coverage. Finally, I propose RightTyper, an efficient and effective type annotation system. RightTyper combines types observed through low-overhead, statistically guided runtime sampling with static analysis and name resolution to produce type annotations comparable in quality to current LLM-based approaches and substantially better than those of all other evaluated tools—while remaining grounded in observed program behavior rather than probabilistic inference. Collectively, these contributions advance the state of the art by showing how low-overhead dynamic analysis helps overcome significant challenges in writing and maintaining reliable Python code.

candidates.title: Data Optimization for LLMs: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted great attention in both academic and industrial communities in recent years. Numerous survey studies have covered various aspects of LLMs, such as learning strategies, applications, alignment, explainability, and evaluation. However, little headway has been made in reviewing data-related aspects for LLMs, despite data being recognized as a key factor contributing to the emergence of the LLMs era. A wide range of data optimization algorithms and techniques are employed in LLMs' training and application processes. These techniques often originate from diverse deep learning domains, with their theoretical inspirations and heuristic motivations appearing unrelated to each other. This study aims to develop a comprehensive framework for LLMs' data optimization techniques to enhance data utilization efficiency. We first discuss data challenges in LLMs' training and inference. Second, we summarize data perception dimensions for evaluating LLMs' data properties. Third, existing optimization techniques are reviewed and categorized into four groups: data selection, augmentation, reweighting, and others. Fourth, we analyze interconnections between these categories. Finally, we identify key challenges and future directions for LLMs' data optimization compared with conventional deep learning approaches.

candidates.title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: An agent's memory must remain useful as information changes across conversations. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. It retrieves relevant versions, places them in source order and labels historical records before passing the evidence to the answer model. Event memory and original dialogue turns provide details missing from structured facts. We evaluated TEM on 420 questions drawn from 600 sessions involving 60 personas. Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71-97.62% overall and 96.67-100.00% on the historical-residence subset. Adding historical labels to otherwise identical, source-ordered facts increased overall hit rates by 17.14-55.95 percentage points. The evidence was compact: 94-118 tokens per answer, or 48.75-56.73% less than session-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A further evaluation on 1,540 LoCoMo questions tested hybrid memory under a fixed evidence budget. TEM exceeded session-aware RAG with both backbones; conservative score differences were 7.92 and 10.58 percentage points. The results support preserving fact versions and exposing their temporal status to the generator when answering questions about repeatedly updated information.

candidates.title: Managing Vector Data for Retrieval Augmented Generation@Dagstuhl Seminar Summary
candidates.abstract: This report summarizes discussions that took place in the context of a Dagstuhl seminar1 to explore the emerging paradigm of AI-native databases designed to support agentic workflows and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with robust database abstractions. The central synthesis of the Dagstuhl discussions is the necessary evolution of databases from passive vector stores into active data-native agentic harnesses that orchestrate AI reasoning and task-centric execution. A recurring lesson across keynotes and working groups is that achieving mission-critical reliability requires integrating AI primitives, such as embeddings, model inference, and semantic operators, as first-class citizens while maintaining traditional database guarantees like transactional consistency, explainability, and cost-aware optimization. This transition necessitates a structured approach to agent memory (spanning episodic, semantic, and procedural scales) and a shift toward adaptive, iterative execution models that go beyond static query planning to accommodate the stochastic nature of foundation models. There is a community consensus that reliability, responsibility, and security (specifically addressing compositional leakage) must be treated as end-to-end concerns supported by holistic benchmarks that evaluate the entire quality chain from retrieval to autonomous action.

candidates.title: A Systematic Review of Hallucination Mitigation in Large Language Models Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become widely used for question answering, education, research, summarization and information support. Despite their usefulness, LLMs may generate false, unsupported or inconsistent information, commonly described as hallucination. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this reliability problem by retrieving relevant information from external knowledge sources and supplying it to the language model as contextual evidence before generating a response. This paper studies the role of RAG in reducing factual hallucinations through a review of existing research and a 50 question pilot comparison of responses generated with and without retrieval support. The submitted report records 49 of 50 responses as correct without RAG and all 50 as correct with RAG; it separately presents a clearly labelled illustrative distribution of 46/3/1 versus 48/2/0 for demonstrating response categories. The distinction is retained to avoid presenting illustrative values as observed experimental results. The study also examines limitations including poor retrieval, unreliable sources, incomplete context and incorrect interpretation of retrieved evidence. The paper concludes that RAG is a practical hallucination-reduction approach, but it should be combined with high-quality retrieval, evidence verification and human oversight for critical applications.

candidates.title: Private Retrieval Augmented Generation via Random Projection
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by querying external structured knowledge. However, it can also introduce privacy risks by leaking sensitive information from the retrieval datastore. We propose a simple method to preserve datastore privacy in RAG systems via random projection. By applying the same projection to both datastore embeddings and query embeddings, our method provably preserves semantic similarity between queries and retrieved items while substantially mitigating data extraction attacks. Across multiple RAG architectures and datasets, we show that this lightweight approach achieves superior retrieval and generation performance compared to prior methods which leverage formal differential privacy (DP) guarantees, while exhibiting comparable empirical privacy under strong attack models. Our results for the first time suggest that random projection can serve as a competitive and practical baseline for privacy-preserving RAG systems.

candidates.title: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): An Adaptive Framework for Evidence-Grounded Question Answering
candidates.abstract: This paper presents a proposed Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for adaptive, evidence-grounded question answering using large language models (LLMs). Unlike conventional single-pass RAG systems, the proposed framework incorporates query planning, retrieval, tool selection, evidence evaluation, answer generation, and self-reflection. The framework uses a bounded feedback loop to improve evidence retrieval when the initial results are insufficient or conflicting. It aims to produce answers supported by relevant source citations while communicating uncertainty when reliable evidence is unavailable. The paper discusses the system architecture, workflow, algorithmic control logic, evaluation methodology, security, privacy, and governance considerations. It also proposes evaluation metrics for answer quality, retrieval effectiveness, factual grounding, latency, computational cost, and component-level ablation studies. Potential applications include research assistance, document question answering, enterprise knowledge management, customer support, and data analysis. This work presents a conceptual framework and proposed evaluation plan. Implementation, benchmark experiments, and measured performance improvements are not reported. Keywords: Agentic RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Large Language Models, AI Agents, Evidence-Grounded Question Answering, Adaptive Retrieval, Self-Reflection.

candidates.title: From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood. This survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem for allocating inference-time resources. We distinguish compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation, from compute-inactive memory, which lies outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, and we characterize offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states on the activation path. On this basis, we formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state transitions within an information lifecycle, and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account. The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.

candidates.title: Data Strategies for Large Language Models: A Unified Perspective on the Training Lifecycle
candidates.abstract: Data strategy plays a central role in training large language models (LLMs). It governs the selection, weighting, and scheduling of training data, thereby determining the capabilities a model can acquire from a fixed data budget. We treat high-quality data as having high training-dependent utility, which depends on the target objective, the model, and its training state rather than on the text alone. Research in this area now spans pretraining and post-training, but related ideas use inconsistent terminology and evaluation protocols. This work reviews data strategies across the training lifecycle and formulates them as policies that allocate a training budget over candidate examples. We organise methods by their decision granularity, model dependence, and temporal adaptivity, then compare their computational requirements and empirical support. Fine-grained or state-dependent policies offer more control but incur additional scoring, search, or rollout costs. Evidence for transfer across model scales and comparable end-to-end cost remains limited. A continuously updated list of papers, along with their public implementations, is available at https://github.com/xuyj233/data_strategy_survey.

candidates.title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bitwidths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and three bit-widths. Furthermore, FPoT can be integrated with state-of-the-art LLM PTQ methods, demonstrating framework-agnostic applicability.

candidates.title: Textbook-Enriched Training for Language Models: Boosting Answer Quality in Specialized Contexts

The evaluation relies on questions from the LARI dataset, which has been validated by human specialists, and combines automatic and qualitative assessment procedures. The findings indicate that small models tuned with structured instructional knowledge achieve stronger semantic alignment and produce more pertinent answers in Portuguese educational QA scenarios.

candidates.title: When Reasoning Is Not Enough: Proactive Inquiry for Cross-Modal Safety in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can act unsafely when individually benign images and texts are interpreted jointly. Beyond implicit reasoning risk, where reasoning drifts toward harm, we identify intent-level risk, where cross-modal ambiguity silently commits the model to a hazardous premise that path-level optimization alone cannot correct. We propose SAFE-PRO, which uses a Risk-Conditioned Uncertainty (RCU) signal, combining predictive entropy with a learned cross-modal risk score, to decide when to ask safety-grounded clarifying questions and where to apply path optimization, under a reward that prioritizes safety and penalizes over-refusal. We also build SSUI-Dialog, a multimodal multi-turn dataset with dual-intent supervision, and theoretically analyze gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk under RCU. Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, SAFE-PRO consistently improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves its over-refusal, and surpasses GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety.

candidates.title: The Expressive Power of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models process vast sequences of input tokens by alternating between classical multi-layer perceptron layers and self-attention mechanisms. While the approximation capabilities of perceptrons are relatively well understood, those of attention mechanisms remain less explored. In this talk, I will compare the proof techniques and approximation results associated with these two types of layers, emphasizing key open questions that connect large language models with approximation theory in infinite-dimensional spaces representing input token distributions.

candidates.title: The Density of Thought: Predicting and Steering Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: We investigate whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. We prompt frozen pretrained models to solve problems via CoT and measure the density of each reasoning step with two independent metrics: LP variance (how unevenly information is distributed across steps, computed as the variance in mean per-token negative log-likelihood) and the Caveman compression ratio. We then test whether density correlates with, and can be steered to improve, answer correctness. Experiments across six model scales, two training paradigms, and 60 GSM8K problems yield four main findings. First, lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models, but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models. Training paradigm therefore appears more influential than model size in determining density behaviour. Second, synthetic experiments reveal an intrinsic complexity preference: models trained on uniformly distributed data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones. Third, direct inference-time density steering reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, indicating that natural density patterns are functionally important to reasoning. Fourth, pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, consistent across both metrics. Finally, we introduce Entropy-Gated Density Routing (EGDR), a self-supervised method using token-level Shannon entropy to gate proportional KVcache adjustments during generation, improving accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without any external guidance.

candidates.title: Name-Bias in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Names carry demographic indicators such as age, gender, and race, which makes them a subtle but strong target of bias in large language models (LLMs). In this work, we present an evaluation of name-based bias across 6 local large language models spanning multiple providers and parameter scales. Using a fill-in-the-blank task, we prompt these models to choose between pairs of first names drawn from U.S. Social Security Administration datasets and a race classification dataset by Rosenman et al.. Our experimental de- sign isolates age and gender effects through balanced name pairings and sentence templates that share a fixed syntactic structure. Across 300,000 local LLM responses, we find consistent and measurable name bias. Models prefer names that are less stereotypically male, older, popular, and white. Furthermore, we find that name-bias is highly sentence-dependent, but not more than associated stereotypes, and gender is the most significant bias, followed by age, name popularity, and race. Our results demonstrate that name-based bias remains pervasive even in local LLMs, highlighting the necessity for standardized evaluation methods and mitigation strategies.

candidates.title: Intelligent generation and propagation prediction of cultural tourism social media content based on diffusion models and multimodal large language models
candidates.abstract: The digital transformation of cultural tourism has intensified the demand for high-quality visual content and accurate prediction of its social media propagation potential. However, existing approaches treat content generation and propagation prediction as isolated tasks, neglecting the coupling between cultural semantic fidelity and viral dissemination. This study proposes a unified framework integrating diffusion models with multimodal large language models (MLLM) to address both challenges jointly. The framework comprises three modules: an MLLM-semantic-guided conditional diffusion generation module with a cross modal conditional injection (CMCI) mechanism for hierarchical semantic control; a content-aware dynamic hypergraph cascade prediction network (CA-DHCNet) that fuses multimodal content features with dynamic hypergraph representations of propagation topology; and a collaborative optimization strategy driven by propagation potential feedback, forming a closed-loop paradigm of "generation–prediction–feedback–regeneration." Experimental results show that, compared to the best baseline method, the proposed method improves cultural semantic consistency by 16.3% and reduces the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) by 12.1%. The prediction module reduces Mean Squared Logarithmic Error by 17.8% on CulTour, while collaborative optimization increases propagation potential scores by 21.1%. These results indicate a positive coupling between high generation quality and high propagation potential, offering a practical solution for intelligent cultural tourism content creation and marketing.

candidates.title: How language model agents reshape price competition
candidates.abstract: Repeated Bertrand competition is a stringent benchmark for algorithmic pricing: in homogeneous-goods markets, standard learning procedures typically select the stage-game Nash outcome with prices near marginal cost. We show that LLM pricing agents can escape this benchmark, depending on deployment decisions. LLMs outperform standard online learners through faster adaptation, but this advantage largely disappears against full-information learners. An extracted surrogate algorithm illustrates how LLMs in specific deployments profit from regularly undercutting slower learners. Agents that post one price every period from raw market histories that include rival prices can sustain supracompetitive regimes in self-play. Agents that periodically emit probability distributions from summarized histories of their own profits instead move toward the competitive region in self-play. Markets mixing these interfaces can generate dynamic regimes in which LLMs establish a high-price anchor and regularly undercut it to capture demand. These regimes can keep both competitors' prices above marginal cost. Deployment choices shape these outcomes, shifting the focus from stationary equilibria to dynamic pricing regimes.

candidates.title: GACC-Bench: Benchmarking Goal-Adaptive Context Compression Ability across Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Context compression in long-running applications of large language models (LLMs) must preserve goal-relevant information, often before specific downstream questions are known. We introduce GACC-Bench, a benchmark for Goal-Adaptive Context Compression that evaluates how reliably LLMs adapt information retention to specified high-level goals. For each source context, we derive one or more high-level goals by grouping source-grounded questions according to shared downstream objectives. The benchmark contains 500 goals and 2,571 questions over 281 document and agent-trace contexts from seven collections spanning diverse domains, with all instances reviewed by human experts. The compressor receives a source context, a goal, and a context-length budget, with the associated evaluation questions withheld. A fixed reader answers these questions individually using the same compressed context. Our evaluation of ten LLM compressors reveals substantial gaps to full-context performance even for the best-performing model, particularly in supporting correct answers to every question associated with a goal. Compared with goal-agnostic compression, target-goal conditioning consistently improves accuracy, whereas mismatched-goal conditioning reduces it. GACC-Bench is available at https://github.com/weiting24/GACC-Bench.

candidates.title: Designing an Amharic Legal Question-Answering System Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: This paper documents the design, implementation and planned evaluation of an Amharic legal question-answering prototype built on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and reports no performance results because the evaluation set it requires has not yet been built. Legal text in Amharic is hard to search, and few retrieval tools support the language. The prototype combines Scrapify, a Python tool that collects and normalizes Amharic web and PDF content, with a Zufan notebook that extracts the Amharic text of the Constitution of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia and defines a LangChain retrieval chain over a Chroma vector store that answers questions with Gemini 2.0 Flash. We describe each pipeline stage as implemented, report descriptive statistics for the 38-page constitutional corpus, and list correctness and reproducibility issues found by auditing the two public notebooks. We then specify a controlled evaluation protocol covering retrieval quality (Recall@k, MRR, nDCG), answer correctness, faithfulness, citation accuracy, abstention on unanswerable questions, and latency. The contribution is a documented baseline and a pre-specified protocol that lets later work measure the reliability of Amharic legal RAG rather than infer it from demonstrations.

candidates.title: MYOPIA: Understanding the Limits of Tree-Based Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Decision trees can make vision-language model (VLM) classification interpretable by replacing a single prediction with a sequence of root-to-leaf questions. However, the accuracy cost of this greedy, non-backtracking procedure remains unclear. We introduce \textbf{MYOPIA}, a benchmark comprising four LLM-generated, human-refined decision trees for GTSRB, MNIST, CIFAR-10, and MSCOCO, together with matched prompts, diagnostic protocols, and an evaluation harness. Across GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA-3.2 11B Vision, tree traversal underperforms zero-shot prompting in all 12 dataset--model pairs; paired bootstrap analyses consistently favor zero-shot. Our diagnostics characterize interacting failure modes associated with this gap. Models often recall tree-encoded class attributes more accurately than they ground the same attributes in images: the mean label--image accuracy gaps are 9.5, 13.8, and 12.6 points for GPT-4o, Qwen-VL Max, and LLaMA, respectively. Incorrect local decisions then irreversibly exclude the correct class, while answer extraction introduces additional model-dependent loss. A node-level audit of the four trees finds that split entropy is weakly but consistently associated with lower node accuracy, whereas depth, branching factor, and within-node grounding differences are less stable. \textbf{MYOPIA} therefore provides a framework for diagnosing hierarchical visual classification and motivates testing tree designs that prioritize perceptual answerability and recovery from early errors. Code is available at https://github.com/islammesabah/VLM_Classification.

candidates.title: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models still struggle to understand 3D spatial relations across views and update spatial judgments as the observer moves. A common approach fuses 3D reconstruction features into visual tokens, but aligning these features with pretrained semantic representations remains challenging under limited spatial supervision. We propose DK-VLM with Dual-Kernel Attention, which computes attention from both a visual token's input position and its geometric position in the scene. A semantic kernel retains the pretrained model's native attention and positional encoding, while a separate geometric kernel uses estimated 3D points and camera poses to directly modulate attention through point displacements and relative view transformations. Then, a learned gate fuses their outputs. Geometry thus enters attention as position rather than as fused reconstruction features. We further introduce Reference-Frame Composition (RC) supervision to train the model to update its reference frame across successive judgments. It provides stepwise turn and heading targets derived from verified single-step annotations. Among the compared methods, DK-VLM-8B achieves the highest average score across six spatial benchmarks and the highest overall scores on VSI-Bench (74.33) and ReVSI-32 (58.28). RC supervision further improves multi-step spatial reasoning, while the full model preserves general video understanding. Project page: https://sumuru789.github.io/DK-VLM-website/.

candidates.title: Beyond Context Length: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Long-context language models support ever longer context windows, and evaluations typically treat context length as the main indicator of difficulty. However, context length alone cannot explain why models fail on long-context tasks that require reasoning over complex information. Contexts of equal length can pose very different challenges: a task may be solvable from a single local passage, or it may require integrating evidence distributed across the full context. We quantitatively characterise this difficulty through three properties: evidence scope, how much necessary information must be found; evidence dispersion, how widely that information is scattered within the context; and reasoning depth, how many dependent steps are needed to derive an answer from it. We construct LURCH, a multi-domain question-answering benchmark of 6,550 instances with supporting evidence and reasoning graphs, enabling all three properties to be quantified. Evaluations of proprietary and open-weight models show that: (1) at fixed context length, all our three properties are strongly negatively correlated with model performance; (2) as context length increases, performance degrades sharply on samples with dispersed evidence, whereas it remains relatively stable on samples with localised evidence; and (3) difficulty compounds across properties, as questions with moderately high values on all three are harder than those with an extreme value on just one. These findings establish evidence scope, dispersion and reasoning depth as measures of long-context reasoning difficulty that complement context length.

candidates.title: Study of the Reliability of Agentic Language Models in Task Execution
candidates.abstract: The reliability of agentic large language models (LLMs) on multi-step tasks, where the model interacts repeatedly with an environment rather than responding in a single exchange, remains an open problem, since a single error at any intermediate step can invalidate an entire task. This thesis examines two connected questions: first, whether improving this reliability through reinforcement learning is feasible on accessible, non-datacenter hardware; second, whether any improvement achieved generalizes beyond the exact training set, or remains narrowly tailored to it. To answer the first question, a complete training pipeline based on the GiGPO (Group-in-Group Policy Optimization) algorithm was implemented end-to-end on a single consumer-grade GPU (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080, 16GB VRAM), from rollout generation to weight updates via LoRA. The method was systematically applied to three open-weight models (llama3.1:8b, qwen2.5:7b, falcon3-7b-instruct) on two task types from AgentBench: Linux (Ubuntu) operating-system interaction, and database interaction. The results show that the answer depends strongly on the model: llama3.1:8b, with the lowest zero-shot baseline, achieved a clear, reproducible improvement on both task types, while qwen2.5:7b, with the highest baseline, remained consistently at a stagnant performance plateau. The third model, falcon3-7b-instruct, with an intermediate baseline, showed a mixed picture: the same stagnant plateau on operating-system tasks, but an active collapse, that is, a gradual loss of competence, on database tasks. Two qualitatively distinct failure mechanisms during training were thereby documented, along with the significant, though not always decisive, effect of how groups in which all rollouts receive exactly the same reward are handled: strictly penalizing such groups can lead to a complete collapse of training, whereas handling them neutrally proved generally safer. Generalization was examined at two levels of effort. First, as an additional, exploratory question, it was checked whether the improvement transfers to a separate, independent benchmark (InterCode): the outcome was asymmetric, with a noticeable drop on Bash tasks and a very small, possibly noise-level improvement on SQL tasks. Second, additional experiments were conducted using a strictly separated split of the data into training, validation, and test sets, rather than the simpler train/validation split used in the remaining experiments, so that the final reported result would be free of peeking bias.

candidates.title: LTM: Latent Transition Based In-Context Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
candidates.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering interactions that are no longer visible. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which stores history as compact latent transitions between consecutive observations. Instantiated on $π_{0.5}$ as LTM-$π$, our method uses a frozen latent action encoder, a lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental inference without memory-specific semantic annotations or external reasoning-model calls. With DreamDojo transitions, LTM-$π$ achieves 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem, performing best among baselines without external reasoning models or memory-specific annotations. Ablations support the contribution of transition content beyond temporal cues and the efficiency of delayed memory admission. Scaling RoboMME demonstrations tenfold improves success from 57.67% to 87.50%, while a Cup Swap diagnostic highlights the role of process supervision in temporal composition. Under a 200-token memory budget, success remains 84.00%, versus 87.50% without compression. Finally, real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency of latent transition memory, highlighting its capacity for complex temporal information, bounded-context operation, and real-world robotic control.

candidates.title: Enabling large language model agents for high-fidelity many-body perturbation theory calculations
candidates.abstract: Many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) methods, including the GW approximation, the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) method, and GW perturbation theory (GWPT), among others, provide accurate first-principles descriptions of excited-state properties and multiparticle interactions of materials. However, their use remains limited due to complex multi-software workflows, interdependent physical parameters, and substantial theoretical expertise. Large language model (LLM) agents, which couple a language model to software tools, show potential in automating computational tasks, but MBPT remains an unaddressed challenge. We show that LLM agents tested in our work, including frontier models such as Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, do not reliably construct MBPT workflows in one attempt, suggesting that correct setup requires expert knowledge and consistency that current models lack. Across tested model-harness combinations, out-of-the-box agents average 54%, 36%, and 19% on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow benchmarks, with strong model dependence and large run-to-run variation. Errors typically originate from cross-stage inconsistencies that surface only several stages after they are introduced. We therefore develop AI-Donkey, an agentic framework that combines expert-curated knowledge with deterministic execution to enable high-fidelity GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT calculations and analyses. With AI-Donkey, all tested agents, from frontier proprietary models to open-weight models, produce complete, runnable MBPT workflows with no observed run-to-run variation. We further demonstrate autonomous calculations and post-processing on 1D, 2D, and bulk materials, including the many-body enhancement of Fröhlich electron-phonon coupling in polar semiconductors. Our approach provides a general framework for knowledge engineering to enable reliable agentic workflows in computational materials science.

candidates.title: Beyond Correctness: Compute-Responsive Data Selection for Reasoning Model Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Reasoning language models increasingly rely on test-time compute scaling, yet most existing work studies how to allocate inference computation while treating the model itself as fixed. We ask a complementary question: can reasoning models be post-trained to make better use of a given amount of test-time compute, and which examples are most useful for this goal? Our key observation is that reasoning problems differ substantially in their response to additional computation. Some are already solved under limited compute, others remain unresolved even after further reasoning, while a distinct subset changes from complete initial failure to success when additional reasoning is provided. We call these compute-responsive (CR) examples and introduce Compute-Responsive Data Selection (CRDS), a post-training data-selection principle that prioritizes examples with empirically demonstrated marginal utility from additional reasoning. On Qwen3-8B, SFT on CR examples recovers 45.3\% of held-out low-compute failures, compared with 40.6\% when training on already-solved examples. The advantage extends beyond the selected CR split: SFT-CR reaches 51.8\% overall accuracy on an independently sampled test distribution, with the gain concentrated on compute-responsive problems. CR training also shifts the compute--accuracy frontier across inference budgets from 512 to 4,096 tokens, outperforming matched non-CR training throughout and reaching 48.1\% recovery at the largest budget. The same pattern is supported across multiple data sources, remains visible under on-policy distillation, and extends to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct when CR sets are reconstructed separately for that model. Better test-time compute utilization can therefore be learned through post-training, with recoverable responses to additional reasoning providing a particularly informative signal for selecting training examples.

candidates.title: The Cost of Context: Profiling the Energy Footprint of Input Tokens in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: The rapid adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and long-context LLMs has shifted the computational burden toward the prefill phase---the initial stage where the model processes all input tokens in parallel before generating a response---yet its energy impact remains poorly characterised. We investigate the contradiction between massive hardware-level power spikes and the sub-linear marginal cost of input tokens reported in system-level studies. Through high-resolution telemetry of Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2 models on NVIDIA A100 hardware, we identify the efficiency threshold where $O(n^2)$ attention complexity overcomes GPU parallelisation. Our results quantify how optimised memory orchestration (PagedAttention) delays this scaling bottleneck across three orders of context scaling, yielding up to an 8.9$\times$ energy efficiency advantage at 112,000 tokens compared to standard baselines. Furthermore, we characterise the energy disparity between input and output tokens, demonstrating that optimised serving (vLLM) causes this ratio to narrow (from $\approx$850$\times$ to 750$\times$) as context scales due to high decode efficiency, whereas unoptimised baselines show a much smaller, roughly constant gap ($\approx$150--230$\times$) because their prefill is itself expensive. This work establishes context-scaling laws that differentiate engine-level optimisations from inherent model constraints, providing an empirical framework for sustainable LLM deployment.

candidates.title: IPF-RAG: temporal-aware retrieval-augmented generation for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis care
candidates.abstract: Personalized clinical management of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is hindered by its complex longitudinal course and fragmented, unstructured data. Although large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) show promise in clinical decision support, current methods face challenges in addressing dynamic disease progression due to static knowledge corpora, a lack of temporal awareness, and susceptibility to semantic noise and hallucinations. To address this, we propose IPF-RAG, a temporal-aware RAG framework for longitudinal IPF care. Driven by a curated dataset of 58 patient trajectories, the framework comprises two core modules. The Temporal Retrieval Module augments semantic matching with temporal-aware evidence anchoring, establishing temporal correlations between disease progression and medical orders. Subsequently, the Structured Enhancement Module integrates this temporal knowledge into structured prompts, applying medical logic constraints to guide LLMs toward evidence-based reasoning. Experiments on internal and external datasets, evaluated by automated assessments and clinical experts, demonstrate that IPF-RAG improves the quality of LLM-generated treatment plans across multiple dimensions. These findings indicate that the proposed approach effectively assists LLMs in clinical decision-making for complex chronic diseases.

candidates.title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
candidates.abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. Context-aware retrieval methods have emerged to address this problem by allowing incremental retrieval from a growing context. However, none of them lets the MLLM learn how to judge what new demonstrations it needs and then carry out progressive retrieval on its own. To this end, we introduce ActICL, which trains an MLLM agent to acquire and use an ICL context via tool-augmented reasoning. An ActICL agent analyzes its own information gaps during iterative reasoning and tool-use actions. Based on these gaps, it performs targeted retrieval to acquire a set of initial candidates. It can then use the existing context to further filter the candidates and refine the context, or it can iteratively perform a new retrieval. When the agent judges that the context is sufficient for the task, or when the resource limit is reached with the user request met, it sends the acquired context to an answering model, either the agent itself or another MLLM. We use a two-stage post-training procedure that jointly optimizes the agent's acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over standard similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points compared to the strongest prior baseline. The contexts acquired by ActICL agents can also be used effectively by frontier models. When GPT-5.6-Sol performs 4-shot ICL, ActICL's contexts improve its performance by 3.5 points over standard retrieval, averaged over three benchmarks.

candidates.title: Analyzing performance of Retrieval Augmented Generation models for Question Answering Tasks
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have become almost a cornerstone of open-domain question answering tasks; in which the quality of answers generated in the process, greatly relies on the effectiveness of retrieval mechanisms. In the realm of LLM, the last two years have seen tremendous progress in RAG architectures, with many models reporting to have improved performance through various design innovations. The cultural question and answering systems of South Asia, in particular, present a specific challenge since the region is home to the vast number of languages and traditions, which are closely interrelated. Along with these deeply intertwined historical narratives increase the need for culturally grounded and context-aware interpretation. Despite major architectural advances in LLMs, claiming significant improvements, challenges remain when answering these region specific questions in native languages. In this study, we aim to extract high-performing factors to guide the development of optimized hybrid RAG systems. We further explore whether the integration of RAG changes performance differently for culturally grounded and non-cultural questions in a South Asian multilingual setup, and whether RAG produces a higher overall percentage of correct answers than contexted answering. We also examine how LLM performance changes when RAG methods are integrated into the question-answering pipeline in comparison with non-contexted and contexted answering and, evaluate whether the introduction of RAG benefits popular or non-popular culturally grounded questions more. Not only does our work evaluate the current methods but also carves a path for future designs of more accurate and efficient question-answering pipelines.

candidates.title: When Is Smaller Greener? Right-Sizing Language Models for Agentic AI
candidates.abstract: AI agents use large language models (LLMs) to plan and act over multiple steps, yet models are usually compared per call rather than per completed task. This paper asks: which model should an agent use to complete tasks reliably while minimising energy, cost and time? We show that per-call comparisons can be misleading for agentic AI. Because a task succeeds only if all required steps succeed, small differences in per-step reliability can produce large differences in overall task success. Failed attempts also consume resources. We therefore evaluate models using energy, cost and time per successfully completed task, treating the completed task as the functional unit. On this basis, we develop a decision model for choosing LLMs in agentic workflows. The model applies to tasks with binary or graded outcomes and to settings with or without retries. We show that each resource has a crossover task length at which a smaller, less reliable model ceases to be the greener, cheaper or faster option. These crossovers divide tasks into three regimes: for short tasks smaller models are preferred, for long tasks larger models are preferred, and only between these extremes do preferences among objectives matter. We embed these results in a two-stage framework that separates efficiency from preference. A Pareto screen first removes models that are never competitive; a weighted decision is required only when a genuine trade-off remains. A pilot study of 15 open-weight models from five developers, ranging from 0.6B to 27B parameters, on two multi-step agent tasks with measured GPU energy supports the predicted structure. The model with the lowest energy per completed task changes with task length and task type, and observed crossover points generally match those predicted from per-step measurements. These findings provide a practical framework for right-sizing language models in agentic AI.

candidates.title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.

candidates.title: GraphRAG-LTM: A Layered Threat Modeling Framework for Attacks on Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) uses document-derived knowledge graphs to assemble evidence for large language model (LLM) answers. Its security depends on both the seed chunks retrieved for a query and the graph evidence assembled from them, yet attacks on this evidence path remain underexplored. We introduce GraphRAG-LTM, a Layered Threat Modeling framework that tests three nested levels of attacker access. BB Query uses ranking feedback to make query edits under a semantic-similarity constraint and demote relevant seed chunks. WB Query uses retriever gradients for the same objective. Graph-aware WB keeps the white-box adversarial query and deletes bridge triplets from the query-specific evidence graph, disrupting multi-hop evidence propagation through localized graph edits. Across datasets, retrievers, and LLM backbones, rank feedback alone reduces answer quality, gradient access strengthens query attacks, and bridge-triplet deletion further impairs supporting-fact retrieval. Further analyses show how seed retrieval and graph evidence jointly contribute to these failures.

candidates.title: When Normalization Hurts: Quantifying Morphological Asymmetry Effects in Arabic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines are increasingly used for Arabic question answering, yet applying morphological normalization to only one side of the query–passage pair has received little systematic study. We examine this normalization asymmetry on Mr. TyDi Arabic (3115 development queries; 2,106,586 passages) with a 2×2 design that applies Farasa segmentation to queries, passages, both, or neither under BM25, alongside dense and hybrid baselines and a fixed Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct reader. Asymmetric normalization reduces nDCG@10 by 10–39%; segmenting only the query costs 3.9× more than segmenting only the passages, and this retrieval pattern replicates on the held-out test split. An analyzer ablation supports the interpretation that segmentation creates the penalty, whereas the directional imbalance arises from its interaction with the Lucene ArabicAnalyzer. In the more damaging direction, the recall deficit persists through k=100, and a score-level diagnostic attributes collapses mainly to displacement by detached affix tokens. Generation metrics also decline significantly; the decline is much smaller than that of retrieval against a passage-prefix reference but roughly two to three times larger when answers are scored against TyDi QA minimal answers. An English-trained dense encoder performs no better than our BM25 configuration, so the large mE5 gain should not be generalized. Within this setting, consistency between query and passage normalization matters more than the choice of symmetric scheme, as the two symmetric schemes do not differ significantly.

candidates.title: What Does LALM Post-training Learn? Rethinking Audio Understanding and Reasoning Capabilities
candidates.abstract: Post-training often improves the performance of large audio-language models on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks. However, these improvements may reflect adaptation to specific question formats, such as multiple-choice questions, rather than genuine advances in audio understanding and reasoning capabilities. To investigate what LALMs actually learn from post-training, we conduct controlled experiments that disentangle improvements in audio understanding from adaptation to specific question formats. Across different models and post-training methods, we find that much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio, but largely disappears when the question format changes. These findings suggest that post-training often teaches models to exploit task-specific textual cues and answer patterns rather than developing generalizable audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.

candidates.title: Single-Pass Decision Scores Enable Rapid Classification with Adjustable Thresholds in Medical Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer binary clinical questions with a yes or no token, leaving the decision threshold implicit and fixed. We derive a continuous score from a single forward pass by renormalizing the probabilities of the yes and no tokens, allowing the threshold to be adapted to clinical needs without retraining. We evaluated this approach with MedGemma and Gemma-3 (4B and 27B) on six medical imaging datasets. The default threshold was frequently misaligned with the task: for identifying normal chest radiographs, MedGemma-27B labeled every image as abnormal, whereas a validation-selected threshold yielded a sensitivity of 0.945 and a specificity of 0.696. Normalization achieved the highest AUROC on four of six datasets (CheXpert: 0.819 vs. 0.777 for raw and 0.743 for text-elicited probabilities), and a single decision required 53-79 ms on one GPU. This simple post-hoc method turns medical MLLMs into fast classifiers with adjustable operating points. Code: https://github.com/TruhnLab/llm-threshold-calibration

candidates.title: RCER: Reconstructing Cross-Evidence Relations for Iterative Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Iterative retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) accumulates knowledge from retrieved evidence to answer complex questions, but existing methods struggle to reconstruct entity correspondences and inferential dependencies across retrieved passages as new information emerges. We propose RCER, an iterative RAG method that reconstructs these cross-evidence relations directly from accumulated source passages. Inter-round relational evidence acquisition identifies entity correspondences and relational dependencies to drive dynamic problem decomposition and iterative retrieval. Reasoning context reconstruction independently constructs a coherent reasoning context through joint selection of complementary passages and derivation of cross-evidence inferences. Cross-evidence compositional reasoning leverages these inferences to establish entity correspondences and compose relations across selected passages for answer derivation. Experiments show that RCER outperforms the best baselines by 2.83 EM and 3.06 F1 points on average across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and achieves superior performance on narrative and implicit reasoning tasks.

candidates.title: Progress-Aware Distillation for Mitigating Stagnation in Small Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency, limiting their practical deployment. To enhance the efficiency of agent systems, recent efforts have focused on transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning-based distillation. Nevertheless, as interaction trajectories grow longer, involving extended reasoning-action chains and extensive environmental feedback, distilled student agents tend to experience progress stagnation: becoming trapped in unproductive loops characterized by persistent failed strategies and difficulty making meaningful progress. Our systematic analysis shows that this phenomenon consistently occurs across diverse SLMs and task domains. To address this issue, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories. ProD encodes the stagnation gap between student and teacher into an adaptive margin for dynamically penalizing possible stagnation. By iteratively applying this procedure, ProD enables student agents to progressively approximate teacher behavior. Extensive experiments involving 8 SLMs, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both the success rates and task-completion efficiency of distilled SLM agents.
